CHOMP and TrajOpt both need an initial trajectory and can stall in bad local minima. In CHOMP's tests, straight-line seeds often beat RRT seeds on the objective where collision removal succeeded; in TrajOpt's, multiple initializations changed success rates <Cite id="ratliff-2009" /><Cite id="schulman-2013" />. The GPU multi-robot planner MR. POP supplies diverse seeds that raise downstream optimizer success, for example from 4% to 72% <Cite id="mr-pop-2026" />.

Ratliff and colleagues describe PRM and RRT as commonly deployed in two phases: find a feasible path, then remove redundant or jerky motion. Schulman and colleagues give trajectory optimization two roles, refining another method's output or planning from scratch <Cite id="ratliff-2009" /><Cite id="schulman-2013" />. Shortcutting, a cheap second stage, repeatedly picks two trajectory points and tries to replace the segment between them with a shorter collision-free one <Cite id="hauser-shortcut-2010" />.

edits.before: Ratliff and colleagues describe PRM and RRT as typically used in a two-phase process: first find a feasible path, then remove redundant or jerky motion. Schulman and colleagues distinguish two roles for trajectory optimization: refining a trajectory generated by another method, or planning from scratch. These papers describe research methods; they do not establish a standard industrial pipeline today <Cite id="ratliff-2009" /><Cite id="schulman-2013" />.
edits.after: As of January 2023, MoveIt 2 recommends Time-Optimal Trajectory Generation (TOTG) for time parameterization <Cite id="moveit-trajectory-processing-2026" />. Because TOTG sets no jerk limits, Ruckig jerk-limited smoothing can follow it as a further post-processing step <Cite id="moveit-time-parameterization-2026" />. PickNik's MoveIt Pro 10.1.0, released September 18, 2026, includes a ProRRT shortcut stage <Cite id="moveit-pro-10-1-2026" />.

edits.before: Sampling planners still label demonstration data, verify that a proposed motion is feasible, and generate the diverse training scenes that [generative simulation](/world-models/generative-sim) pipelines rely on. Optimization survives inside model-predictive control, which replans a short horizon at every control cycle, a design whose tradeoffs against learned policies have their own module in [reward design and the MPC debate](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc). Hierarchical robot learning, from SayCan onward, lets a learned system emit goals for a classical planner to execute; end-to-end policies learn to plan within the policy.
edits.after:
Motion Policy Networks trained on over 3 million motion planning problems in over 500,000 [environments](/world-models/generative-sim) <Cite id="mpinets-2022" />. Neural MP distills motion-planner data into a reactive generalist policy and adds lightweight optimization for safety. Its authors report success gains of 23%, 17% and 79% over sampling, optimization and learning-based planners <Cite id="neural-mp-2024" />.

Deep Reactive Policy replaced AIT\* with cuRobo as its expert planner because GPU acceleration let it scale to 10 million expert trajectories. Its authors report that AIT\* achieved 0% success on all dynamic tasks, and cuRobo fell to 3.00% when the goal was temporarily obstructed <Cite id="deep-reactive-policy-2025" />.

edits.before: What end-to-end policies do not escape is the geometry. A diffusion policy's action chunk is a trajectory in configuration space; an RRT's path is a trajectory in configuration space. The difference is who computed it, a planner with an explicit collision model or a network with an implicit one. The modules that follow, [control](/classical/control) and state estimation, assume some such trajectory exists and ask how to track it and where the robot actually is while doing so.
edits.after: Receding-horizon model-predictive control keeps optimization inside the feedback loop <Cite id="mayne-2000" />; [reward design and the MPC debate](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc) weighs it against learned policies. Diffusion Policy represents a visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising diffusion process run with receding-horizon control <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />. [Control](/classical/control) and state estimation track the resulting trajectories and locate the robot.

edits.before: A deployable planner consumes more than a start and goal. It needs the robot model, current state, collision geometry, allowed contacts, attached objects, joint limits, timing limits and a controller capable of executing the returned trajectory. Give each input a freshness rule. A collision-free path against a stale scene is not a safe path, and a valid geometric path can still violate velocity or torque limits after time parameterization.
edits.after: A deployable planner needs the robot model, current state, collision geometry, allowed contacts, attached objects, joint and timing limits and a controller that can execute the result. A path checked against a stale scene is unsafe. TOTG time-parameterizes a path, computing the time-optimal trajectory that exactly follows a differentiable joint-space path within velocity and acceleration bounds <Cite id="totg-2012" />. Ruckig adds real-time jerk-limited generation; its authors tested it on over 1,000,000,000 random trajectories <Cite id="ruckig-2021" />. The cuRoboV2 authors note that fast planners output physically unexecutable trajectories, and report 99.7% success under a 3 kg payload against 72 to 77% for baselines <Cite id="curobo-v2-2026" />.

seeAlso: - "manipulation/vla-models" - "data-hardware/hardware-taxonomy" --- import { PerceptionErrorBudget } from '@/components/interactive/perception-error-budget'; Perception for manipulation is the pipeline that turns camera and depth data into object poses in the robot's own frame. [Grasp planning](/classical/grasp-planning) computes force closure against a known object pose, which assumes perception has already located the object to a tolerance the gripper can act on. This article groups an explicit perception pipeline into six stages for explanation; that organization is not a universal architecture or a required fixed execution order. Calibrate the camera so a pixel means a direction. Calibrate it against the robot so that direction means something in the robot's frame. Measure depth so the direction becomes a point. Detect and segment so points become an object. Estimate pose so the object becomes a graspable rigid body. The instrument below combines three adjustable error magnitudes by root-sum-of-squares as an illustrative modelling choice. It does not establish that calibration, depth and pose errors are statistically independent, or that its output bounds the positioning error of a real pipeline. ## An illustrative positioning budget The instrument combines three authored input magnitudes labelled hand-eye, depth and pose. In this model only, depth is evaluated at a fixed 0.5 m nominal distance and the pose input is held constant during a distance sweep. The hand-eye proxy uses the ray-to-plane geometry defined below; it is not the full error of a rigid transform. With the default opaque-target, depth and pose settings and a half-degree angle, the hand-eye contribution is small at 15 cm and largest at 1.5 m. The far-end readout falls in the marginal model band; it is not a prediction that a real grasp will succeed or jam. Slide the working-distance control and the hand-eye term grows toward its 1.5 m maximum. The model's 15 mm band comes from an authored geometry: a 90 mm opening centred around a 60 mm part leaves $(90-60)/2=15$ mm on each side. Its bands at 15 mm and 30 mm are teaching thresholds. They have no measured grasp-tolerance or success/failure basis. A separate assembly example reports 0.5 mm clearance ; that reported setting does not validate this calculator or establish a general limit for vision-based positioning.
The next sections use those six chosen stages to organize the discussion; the calculator is a separate illustrative model. ## Calibration: what a pixel means A camera is a device that discards a dimension. It maps a 3D point onto a 2D sensor, and the mapping it uses is described by the intrinsics: focal length in pixels on each axis, the principal point, and the lens distortion terms. Before those are known, a pixel coordinate is a number with no geometric meaning. Zhang's 2000 method uses a planar calibration target. Show the camera a planar target at several arbitrary orientations, none of them measured; the paper models radial lens distortion and gives a closed-form solution followed by nonlinear refinement under a maximum-likelihood criterion . Zhang compares this setup with classical techniques that use expensive equipment such as two or three orthogonal planes. Extrinsics are the other half: where the camera sits relative to something else. Two cameras on a stereo rig need their relative pose. A camera and a robot need the harder version. ### Hand-eye calibration: what a pixel means to the robot A perfectly calibrated camera reporting perfectly accurate 3D points in the *camera's* frame is useless to an arm that plans in its *own* frame. Hand-eye calibration is the step that connects them: for a wrist-mounted camera, the rigid transform from the gripper flange to the camera; for a camera bolted to a post, the transform from the robot base to the camera. The 1989 papers on it share one form: move the robot through a set of known motions while the camera watches a static target, and each motion pair gives you an equation of the form $AX = XB$, where $A$ is the robot's motion, $B$ is the camera's observed motion, and $X$ is the unknown transform. Tsai and Lenz gave the efficient closed-form technique still used, solving rotation first and then translation from the accumulated constraints . The instrument uses an illustrative ray-to-plane model. It does not calculate the full three-dimensional hand-eye error. Here $d$ is the separation along the normal to a target plane, and $\theta$ is the inclination of a ray relative to that normal. The lateral intersection offset used by the instrument is $$ e_\theta(d) = d \, \tan \theta $$ With $d$ expressed in millimetres, the local example at one degree gives about 1.7 mm at 10 cm and 17 mm at 1 m. These are evaluations of the authored formula. The calibration paper does not report them as measurements, and they do not predict grasp success. The formula is not a general norm of a rigid-transform error; nor is an exact tangent construction the same claim as a small-angle approximation. ## Depth sensing: what fails, and on what The examples below report specifications and limitations of named devices. A universal accuracy or speed ranking across sensing technologies would need different evidence. **Stereo** matches features between two images and triangulates. It needs texture: the matching is a correspondence search, so a featureless surface gives it nothing to correspond. The March 2026 RealSense D400-series datasheet lists ±2% Z-accuracy for D410/D415 and D43x at distances up to 2 m, with an 80% region of interest at HD resolution. Its range table gives different limits for other model groups: up to 4 m for D450/D455/D455f/D456 and up to 0.5 m for D401/D405. Depth accuracy compares valid pixels with ground truth. Factory KPIs reflect typical conditions and can change with the environment. The D405 protocol uses a textured target in typical room light (about 250 lux); the other models use a texture-less white target, default 150 mW laser power and auto exposure. The measurement region covers 80% of the depth field of view, leaving the rest outside that guarantee . RealSense's tuning checklist for the D415 and D435 says that D400 depth error scales as the square of distance. It advises moving closer where possible, but staying outside the minimum operating distance, MinZ. The guide also describes resolution and range trade-offs when changing MinZ, and notes that focus and different left/right views can limit very-near-range matching . A pattern projector is the standard mitigation, painting texture onto surfaces that have none . **Industrial 3D scanning.** The PhoXi 3D Scanner L product page separately lists calibration accuracy of 0.200 mm (1 σ), temporal noise of 0.190 mm (1 σ), a scanning range of 870 to 2150 mm, and a scanning time of 250 to 2750 ms. The separate range field does not establish uniform accuracy throughout that range. These named-model specification fields give no family-wide ranking, per-material accuracy guarantee or robot control frequency . **Time of flight** measures the round-trip of modulated light per pixel. It works without texture, but multi-path interference can cause one pixel to integrate light that arrived by more than one route. Microsoft's Azure Kinect DK documentation lists five reasons for invalid depth pixels: outside the active IR illumination mask, saturated IR signal, low IR signal, filter outlier, and multi-path interference. Such pixels have a depth value of zero to mark invalid data; the surface has not been measured at zero distance. Under ambiguous depth, the page describes light reflecting from one wall onto another in a corner, and mixed foreground/background signals around object edges. It also notes that fast motion can increase edge invalidation because of the raw-depth exposure interval . ### The failure taxonomy that decides how a cell is built The examples below distinguish material-related problems from weak signal, ambiguous stereo correspondence and view-dependent invalidation. The RealSense and Azure Kinect guidance describes particular sensors and setups. Other depth-sensing families need their own evaluation on these surfaces. - **Transparent** surfaces refract light, so the sensor ranges whatever is behind them. Transparent objects "often appear as noisy or distorted approximations of the surfaces that lie behind them", which is the premise the ClearGrasp work was built on: it infers surface normals, transparent-surface masks and occlusion boundaries and then *replaces* the depth the sensor returned . - **Specular reflections.** The RealSense datasheet says they “May cause image saturation” on D400, while the D400f column says “Saturation mitigated”. Saturation can still occur . The time-of-flight documentation lists saturated IR signal as an invalidation cause in its own right . - **Dark surfaces and low signal.** Azure Kinect can invalidate a pixel when its IR signal is too weak to generate depth . RealSense's D415/D435 guidance relates D4xx depth quality to the input images and describes grainy images in low light. It warns about both underexposure and overexposure. Active illumination changes the setup: for its projected-pattern example, reducing background light while leaving the projector on can improve the pattern's signal-to-noise ratio . These are signal, exposure and illumination conditions; a visibly dark object does not always lose depth. - **Thin objects versus repetitive structures.** RealSense names fences and wire grids as repetitive scenes in which left/right correspondence can become ambiguous. Its D4 processor compares the best and second-best match scores; similar scores can indicate aliasing even when they differ. Increasing DSSecondPeakThreshold rejects more results as black or zero depth. This guidance concerns repetitive-pattern matching; it makes no blanket failure claim for every thin object . - **Self-occlusion versus view-dependent invalidation.** In its multi-path discussion, the Azure Kinect documentation says that a surface area invalidated from one camera view may reappear from another. This view-dependent multi-path example does not establish recovery of every missing surface by multi-view capture or describe generic self-occlusion . The 2 percent is measured against a texture-less white target with the laser projector at default power ; the 0.200 mm specification publishes no target condition . An accuracy figure for a transparent or specular surface is not disclosed in these datasheets. That absence gives no error estimate for those materials. Research on transparent-object depth addresses the missing measurements. Once you have depth you have a point cloud, and a network that consumes one has to be invariant to the ordering of its own input, since the set carries no canonical order. PointNet solved that with a shared per-point encoder and a symmetric pooling function . PointNet++ groups metric-space neighbourhoods and applies PointNet within them, building local features at progressively larger scales. It uses sampled centroids, radius-based neighbourhoods and coordinates relative to each centroid; pooling summarizes the local features, losing some geometry. Small neighbourhoods can contain too few samples, so its density-adaptive variants combine information across scales . ## Detection: from pixels to candidate objects Classical detection returns boxes over a class list fixed at training time, which is a poor fit for a robot that will be asked about objects nobody enumerated. Open-vocabulary detection removes the fixed list. Grounding DINO extends the DINO detector with language and vision fusion in the feature enhancer, language-guided query selection and cross-modality decoder. It accepts category names or referring expressions; the paper reports weak referring-expression performance without REC training data . The reported 52.5 AP on COCO 2017 validation is for Grounding DINO L with a Swin-L backbone, pretrained on O365, OpenImage and GoldG without COCO training images. Here, zero-shot transfer excludes COCO’s training split. Its object categories may still occur in pretraining . DINOv2 learns image and patch features through self-supervised pretraining on the curated LVD-142M image dataset. Its transfer evaluations keep the image encoder frozen while training task-specific predictors: linear classifiers for image classification and semantic segmentation, and linear or DPT depth heads. “Without fine-tuning” describes the encoder; downstream predictors are trained . ## Segmentation: the grounding layer A box around a mug also contains the table behind it. A grasp planner needs a surface region, which per-pixel labelling can provide. Segment Anything (SAM, 2023) makes image segmentation *promptable*. Its default ViT-H model was trained on SA-1B, which the paper reports as 1.1 billion automatically generated masks from 11 million images. Those are dataset counts: the training recipe samples and filters masks, with no accounting of every mask used. Points, boxes and mask prompts condition the decoder; an ambiguous point can refer to a part or a whole object, so SAM can return multiple candidate masks . The paper evaluates zero-shot transfer on new datasets and tasks. In its single-point test across 23 datasets, the default prompt is the ground-truth mask's center and the default output is SAM's most confident mask. SAM has higher mIoU than RITM on 16 of those 23 datasets; the separate oracle result selects the best mask using ground truth. Free-form text is a separately trained, CLIP-conditioned proof of concept. The ordinary geometric-prompt model has no demonstrated equivalent text capability. Fine structures and boundaries remain failure cases. The reported roughly 50 ms prompt processing on a browser CPU assumes a precomputed image embedding; the paper explicitly says a heavy image encoder prevents overall real-time performance . SAM 2 extends point, box and mask prompting across video with a streaming memory of earlier predictions and prompted frames. The paper dated 28 October 2024 states that its reported results use the improved model called SAM 2.1. In the interactive video experiment, the authors report better average segmentation accuracy with more than three times fewer interactions than their SAM+XMem++ and SAM+Cutie baselines. This is a simulated comparison on nine densely annotated video datasets, using Hiera-B+ at resolution 1024, three clicks per interacted frame and one to eight interacted frames. Actual user effort was not measured. Offline evaluation repeatedly prompts the worst-IoU frame; online evaluation adds corrections when IoU falls below 0.75 and changes only subsequent frames. Both use ground truth to select corrections. The main description feeds tracker masks to SAM as mask prompts; the appendix instead reconstructs masks with clicks until IoU exceeds 0.8, then adds correction clicks. Those baseline descriptions do not fully agree . The image-speed comparison is different. The paper compares SA-1B-only SAM 2 with a Hiera-B+ encoder against SAM with ViT-H: 58.9 versus 58.1 one-click mIoU on the 23-dataset SA-23 aggregate, and 130.1 versus 21.7 images per second. That is the paper's roughly sixfold throughput result on one A100, with image batches of 10, PyTorch 2.3.1, CUDA 12.1, bfloat16 mixed precision and compiled image encoders for both models. The result measures batched image throughput; single-image latency, video-tracking speed and robot control frequency need separate measurements. The image evaluation spans 37 datasets, including video frames treated as individual images; the separate first-frame-prompt video-object-segmentation comparison spans 17 datasets . These are model- and protocol-specific results. Objects are inferred independently, which limits inter-object modeling. The paper still reports failures after shot changes or long occlusions, in crowded scenes and on thin, fast-moving details. Its mixed-data SA-23 prose says 61.4 while the image tables say 61.9; that unresolved source inconsistency concerns the mixed-data model, while the comparison above uses SA-1B-only training. The paper also warns that OVIS is not strictly zero-shot for the mixed-data model because its videos occur in MOSE training data . Promptable segmentation supplies object masks in MOKA and ReKep, but the [keypoint interfaces](/manipulation/hierarchical) do not all use the same perception stack. MOKA uses GroundedSAM masks to propose marked candidate points, then prompts a pretrained VLM to select grasp, function and target keypoints where applicable, along with waypoint regions and motion attributes. Calibrated depth lifts the surface points into the robot frame; a separate grasp sampler and motion pipeline turn the selections into actions. The prompted method does not train a robot policy, although the paper separately studies policy distillation from successful trajectories . ReKep proposes semantic keypoints from DINOv2 features within SAM masks and calibrated RGB-D geometry. GPT-4o writes Python sub-goal and path constraints from a marked image and a language instruction; a separate solver repeatedly plans end-effector motion from tracked keypoints. Its implementation penalizes constraint violations rather than guaranteeing physical feasibility. Rigidity assumptions and tracking failures remain limitations, and some evaluations use human annotations or disable tracking . RoboPoint instruction-tunes a VLM to predict image-space affordance points, mixing synthetic object and free-space reference data with real-image VQA and LVIS detection data. Its point predictor works without an external detector at test time; the reported robot pipeline still uses depth, an end-effector offset and a motion planner. A predicted point needs those additional steps to become a grasp pose or control policy . Dense Object Nets learns a descriptor vector for each RGB pixel, using matches from static RGB-D reconstructions as self-supervision. With object-centric training techniques, the authors demonstrate correspondence across viewpoints and moderately deformable object configurations; they do not guarantee that every physical point has an identical descriptor. Their class-consistent training mode generalizes across sufficiently similar hats, shoes and mugs, while instance-specific training distinguishes objects . The paper's 20-minute estimate is for learning a new object, including collection of a handful of scenes. Its optimization report gives 3500 steps, about 13 minutes, on a single Nvidia 1080 Ti or Titan Xp; a separate static-scene scan takes about 70 seconds. The demonstrated setup uses a calibrated Kuka IIWA LBR arm, a wrist-mounted Primesense Carmine 1.09 RGB-D sensor and a Schunk two-finger gripper. Humans often rearranged objects and still switched and identified different objects during multi-object collection. A matched reference pixel is mapped into depth geometry for grasp planning; the gripper's 6-DoF orientation requires additional information . Dex-Net 2.0 learns to score candidate parallel-jaw grasps. The paper reports 6.7 million synthetic training datapoints pairing grasps with depth observations and analytic grasp-quality labels, generated from 1500 object models. Its training images are grasp-aligned crops, described as “over 6.7 million grasp images.” They do not count measured robot successes or necessarily distinct scene views. GQ-CNN takes an aligned depth crop and the gripper's depth relative to the camera. Its labels use thresholded robust epsilon quality and collision constraints; physical grasp success is evaluated separately . The Dex-Net planner samples and ranks antipodal candidates, checks reachability and table collision, and operates on single-view depth for an isolated object on a planar worksurface. Training assumes rigid objects and known camera intrinsics and gripper geometry, including synthetic object models. Execution does not register a target-specific object model. Missing depth on thin parts and collisions remain failure modes; its pile-handling demonstration separates objects before grasping . ## 6-DoF pose estimation, and how to read a claim about it Pose estimation is the stage that turns a mask into a rigid body with an orientation. The methods divide by what they assume they already know about the object, which is also the division that decides whether you can use one. **Instance-level** methods are trained for specific objects. PoseCNN localises each object's centre, predicts its distance, and regresses a quaternion for rotation, with a loss designed to handle symmetric objects; it shipped with the YCB-Video dataset, 21 objects across 92 videos and 133,827 frames . Accurate on the objects it knows, useless on the object that arrived this morning. **Model-free and novel-object** methods removed that constraint. MegaPose estimates the pose of novel objects by render-and-compare against a CAD model supplied at test time , and FoundationPose unifies model-based and model-free operation in one network: give it a CAD model, or give it a handful of reference images, and it runs on an object it never trained on, reaching results comparable to instance-level methods despite assuming far less . To read a pose-estimation result, check its evaluation protocol. Hinterstoisser and colleagues' LINEMOD-based paper evaluates a model $\mathcal M$ using its ground-truth rotation and translation $(R,T)$ and its estimated pose $(\tilde R,\tilde T)$. Equation (1) averages the distances between corresponding model points after the two transforms
: $$ m = \operatorname{avg}_{x \in \mathcal M} \lVert (Rx+T)-(\tilde R x+\tilde T) \rVert $$ The paper counts the detection and pose estimate as correct when $m \leq k_m d$, where $d$ is the model's diameter and $k_m$ is a chosen coefficient. Equality counts as correct. Table 1 uses $k_m=0.1$ for this evaluation; other evaluations may choose another threshold
. For the symmetry-aware pose error, Equation (2) changes the correspondence rule: each ground-truth-transformed model point is matched to its nearest estimated-pose-transformed model point, and those distances are averaged
: $$ m = \operatorname{avg}_{x_1 \in \mathcal M} \min_{x_2 \in \mathcal M} \lVert (Rx_1+T)-(\tilde R x_2+\tilde T) \rVert $$ The paper uses this rule for objects that are ambiguous, or appear ambiguous from a subset of views, naming “cup”, “bowl”, “box” and “glue”
. The rule operates on supplied model points; an indistinguishable rotation of another bowl may still have nonzero error or fail the chosen threshold. The BOP Challenge 2023 report uses a different aggregate from ADD-S. For 6-DoF localisation, each dataset score first averages three metric recalls: VSD, MSSD and MSPD. Each recall is averaged over multiple correctness thresholds, with a strict correctness test $e < \theta_e$; VSD also varies its misalignment tolerance. $AR_C$ then averages the dataset scores equally across seven core datasets: LM-O, T-LESS, ITODD, HB, YCB-V, TUD-L and IC-BIN. The report displays this dimensionless recall score on a 0 to 100 scale. ADD-S distance, millimetres and robot success are separate quantities. Its 2D-detection $AP_C$ uses object-first averaging instead. VSD considers the visible object surface; MSSD and MSPD use pre-identified object symmetries. The report delegates numerical threshold grids and further symmetry details to its cited 2020 report. Seen and unseen localisation use the same evaluation methodology, with object identities and instance counts supplied at test time
. In the report’s retrospective 2017 to 2023 comparison, seen-object accuracy rises from 56.9 to 85.6 $AR_C$, a relative improvement of more than 50 percent. The endpoints are Vidal’s point-pair-feature method and GPose2023. They measure benchmark accuracy; robot performance is a different outcome. The dates and channels need care: Figure 1 labels the selected methods RGB-D and associates Vidal with 2017, while Table 2 labels the Vidal-Sensors18 entry’s submission year as 2019 and its test input as depth. That entry uses PPF and ICP without training images; GPose2023 uses object-specific networks, custom detections, coordinate-guided refinement and RGB-D training/testing with PBR plus real training images
. For unseen objects, GenFlow-MultiHypo16 leads Task 4 with 67.4 $AR_C$. The best 2020 seen-object entry, CosyPose-ECCV20-SYNT+REAL-ICP, scores 69.8 in Task 1. The report calls these results comparable, with distinct evaluation tracks. Their reported average image-processing times are 34.58 and 13.74 seconds, respectively. Hardware is not matched for a speed ratio, and these times do not measure robot control frequency. Both entries test on RGB-D images. GenFlow uses one network across datasets, CNOS-fastSAM, recurrent-flow refinement and PBR training; CosyPose uses dataset-specific networks, default synthetic-plus-real detections, DeepIM plus ICP refinement and RGB training with PBR plus real images. Task 4 still supplies 3D mesh models of the test objects for onboarding, capped at 5 minutes per object on one GPU; no real images of those objects may be used for onboarding. The distinct training and onboarding conditions prevent this comparison from establishing that the seen-versus-unseen gap disappeared. The report still shows GenFlow failures under heavy object occlusion
. ## Visual servoing: image-based and position-based control Image-based visual control defines a desired configuration of image features and uses their measured error to guide motion. Espiau, Chaumette and Rives’s 1992 paper applies a task-function framework to this problem. The task function is designed for regulation and need not be the raw feature difference. Their interaction matrix relates feature rates to the camera’s translational and rotational velocity relative to the scene, expressed in the camera frame. Convergence depends on the task and interaction-model conditions; neglecting target motion can leave a tracking error . For the fixed goal and motionless target considered in Chaumette and Hutchinson’s Part I, the relation is $\dot{s} = L_s v_c$: $v_c$ is the camera’s six-component spatial velocity, not a vector of joint rates . Visual servoing uses vision in the control loop; image-based visual servoing (IBVS) and position-based visual servoing (PBVS) define different errors. IBVS uses image features, while PBVS uses estimated pose parameters. This does not make IBVS universally pose- or calibration-free: the point-feature interaction matrix uses depth and camera intrinsics, and its estimate may use current depths or depths at the desired pose
. For a fixed goal and motionless target, the tutorial gives local asymptotic stability conditions for redundant-feature IBVS: the interaction matrices must have full rank, and the estimated pseudoinverse multiplied by the true matrix must satisfy a positivity condition. The approximations must not be too coarse. Within a convergent IBVS motion, coarse estimates can change the camera trajectory without changing the final pose reached; poor estimates can instead make the system unstable. Large displacements can encounter local minima or singularities, and the camera path can be unpredictable and suboptimal. This is not a guarantee under arbitrary calibration error or image noise. In PBVS, errors in the estimated pose can also affect final accuracy
. Chaumette and Hutchinson’s Part I, *Basic Approaches* (2006), presents IBVS and PBVS and analyzes their performance and stability
. Part II, *Advanced Approaches* (2007), extends the treatment to interaction-matrix estimation, hybrid and partitioned control, optimization, switching, trajectory planning, target tracking, and joint-space formulations for eye-in-hand and eye-to-hand systems
. Visibility requirements depend on the chosen measurements. The tutorial’s stereo point feature is observed in both images
, while its epipolar estimate uses matches between the current and desired images. Part II describes switching and trajectory-planning methods that address target visibility, occlusions and joint limits
. Visibility is not automatic: Part I gives PBVS configurations in which points leave the camera’s field of view
. ## Separate model error from geometric error Evaluate a perception model in its native output first, then evaluate the geometry that consumes it. A detector can have stable image coordinates while the robot misses because the camera transform drifted. A depth model can improve pixel metrics while a grasp degrades because invalid values cluster on the target material. Mixing the stages into one task-success number makes both failures harder to localize. Maintain a small calibration target set and a separate task object set. Track reprojection, depth residual, pose residual, age and task success as a chain, preserving sample IDs between stages. Re-run the geometric checks after camera remounts, lens changes, time-source changes and software updates that alter resizing or intrinsics. The dedicated [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) defines those checks; the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) shows where images, transforms and timestamps meet at runtime. ## What the end-to-end models replaced This is the argument the module exists to make. Every stage above is a place where a real system carries an interface, a calibration file, a failure mode and an engineer who owns it. The six stages chosen here name different interfaces: camera calibration, hand-eye calibration, depth, detection, segmentation and pose estimation. That authored grouping is an editorial guide, not an exhaustive subsystem count or proof that their errors form one statistical budget. The explicit pipeline is exactly what end-to-end vision-language-action policies replaced. A policy trained on images and actions does not compute a pose, because nothing in its objective asks it to, and the geometric reasoning that calibration and pose estimation made explicit gets absorbed into weights where it is no longer a stage you can inspect or calibrate. That trade runs in both directions. What you buy is a stack that no longer breaks when an object arrives that no detector was trained on and no CAD model exists for. What you sell is the error budget: when an end-to-end policy misses a grasp by 8 mm, there is no hand-eye residual to re-solve, because there is no hand-eye transform. The [keypoint interfaces](/manipulation/hierarchical) sat in the honest middle of that trade, and what happened to them is worth noting. They kept geometry as an explicit intermediate representation while letting a learned model produce it, and by the time frontier systems arrived the geometry had moved out of the runtime pipeline and into the training mixture as an auxiliary objective. Naming this pipeline is what makes that history legible instead of mystical. When comparing an end-to-end policy with an explicit pipeline, ask which interfaces remain explicit. The six-stage grouping here is one way to organize that question, not a required decomposition of every policy.

Azure Kinect invalidates a pixel whose IR signal is too weak to generate depth . RealSense ties D4xx depth quality to the input images and warns of grainy low-light images, underexposure and overexposure. For its projected-pattern example, reducing background light with the projector on can raise the pattern's signal-to-noise ratio . - RealSense names fences and wire grids as scenes where left-right correspondence can become ambiguous. Its D4 processor compares the best and second-best match scores, and raising DSSecondPeakThreshold rejects more matches as zero depth . - Azure Kinect notes that a surface invalidated by multi-path from one camera view can reappear from another . The 2% figure is measured on a texture-less white target with the projector at default power , and the PhoXi page publishes no target condition for its 0.200 mm figure . Accuracy for transparent or specular surfaces is not disclosed in either datasheet. Depth yields a point cloud, an unordered set that a network must process without depending on input order. PointNet uses a shared per-point encoder and a symmetric pooling function . PointNet++ applies PointNet within radius neighbourhoods around sampled centroids, in coordinates relative to each centroid, building local features at growing scales. Density-adaptive variants combine scales where small neighbourhoods hold too few samples . ## Detection: from pixels to candidate objects Classical detectors return boxes over a class list fixed at training time. Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN with a branch that predicts an object mask in parallel with box recognition . Open-vocabulary detection removes the fixed list. Grounding DINO adds language-vision fusion to the DINO detector's feature enhancer, query selection and decoder, and accepts category names or referring expressions. It performs weakly on referring expressions without REC training data. Its Swin-L model reports 52.5 AP on COCO 2017 validation after pretraining on O365, OpenImage and GoldG without COCO training images . OWLv2 self-trains on web image-text pairs at over 1B examples. With an L/14 model this raised AP on LVIS rare classes, which had no human box annotations, from 31.2% to 44.6% . Grounding DINO 1.5 Edge reaches 75.2 FPS with TensorRT at 36.2 zero-shot AP on LVIS-minival . DINOv2 learns image and patch features by self-supervised pretraining on the curated LVD-142M dataset. Its transfer evaluations freeze the encoder and train linear heads for classification and segmentation, and linear or DPT heads for depth . DINOv3 adds Gram anchoring against the degradation of dense feature maps during long training . ## Segmentation: the grounding layer A box around a mug also contains the table behind it, so a grasp planner needs the surface region that per-pixel labelling provides. Segment Anything (SAM, 2023) makes segmentation *promptable*. Its default ViT-H model was trained on SA-1B, reported as 1.1 billion automatically generated masks on 11 million images. Point, box and mask prompts condition the decoder, and an ambiguous point can return several candidate masks for a part or a whole object . In SAM's single-point test across 23 datasets, the prompt is the ground-truth mask's center and the output SAM's most confident mask, which beats RITM's mIoU on 16. Free-form text was a separately trained, CLIP-conditioned proof of concept, and the geometric-prompt model has no demonstrated text capability. Fine structures and boundaries remain failure cases. The prompt step of about 50 ms on a browser CPU assumes a precomputed embedding, and the heavy image encoder prevents overall real-time performance . SAM 3 (2025) takes concept prompts, short noun phrases or image exemplars, and returns masks and identities for every matching instance. Its data engine produced 4M unique concept labels, and its authors report doubling the accuracy of existing systems on image and video concept segmentation . SAM 2 extends prompting to video with a streaming memory of earlier predictions and prompted frames, and its October 2024 paper reports results for SAM 2.1. Its simulated interactive tests on nine video datasets use Hiera-B+ at resolution 1024 and three clicks per interacted frame. There the authors report better accuracy with over three times fewer interactions than SAM+XMem++ and SAM+Cutie; actual user effort was not measured. On images, the SA-1B-only Hiera-B+ model scores 58.9 one-click mIoU on SA-23 against SAM ViT-H's 58.1. It processes 130.1 images per second against 21.7, about six times the throughput on one A100 with image batches of 10, bfloat16 and compiled encoders. The image evaluation spans 37 datasets . Objects are inferred independently, and failures persist after shot changes or long occlusions, in crowded scenes and on thin, fast-moving details . Grounded SAM feeds Grounding DINO's open-set boxes to SAM and reports 48.7 mean AP on the zero-shot SegInW benchmark . CNOS segments unseen objects by matching DINOv2 descriptors of SAM proposals against references built from CAD models, surpassing prior methods by 19.8% AP on BOP's seven core datasets . Promptable segmentation supplies object masks to MOKA and ReKep, two [keypoint interfaces](/manipulation/hierarchical) with different perception stacks. MOKA uses GroundedSAM masks to propose marked candidate points, then prompts a pretrained VLM to select grasp, function and target keypoints, waypoint regions and motion attributes. Calibrated depth lifts the points into the robot frame, and a separate grasp sampler and motion pipeline produce actions; the prompted method trains no robot policy, though the paper separately studies distilling successful trajectories into one . ReKep proposes semantic keypoints from DINOv2 features within SAM masks and calibrated RGB-D geometry. A large vision-language model writes Python sub-goal and path constraints from a marked image and an instruction, and a solver repeatedly plans end-effector motion from tracked keypoints. The solver penalizes constraint violations without guaranteeing physical feasibility, and rigidity assumptions and tracking failures remain limitations. Some evaluations use human annotations or disable tracking . RoboPoint instruction-tunes a VLM to predict image-space affordance points from synthetic object and free-space data mixed with real-image VQA and LVIS detection data. It needs no external detector at test time, though its robot pipeline adds depth, an end-effector offset and a motion planner . Dense Object Nets learns a descriptor for each RGB pixel, self-supervised by matches from static RGB-D reconstructions, and demonstrates correspondence across viewpoints and moderately deformable configurations. Class-consistent training generalizes across sufficiently similar hats, shoes and mugs, while instance-specific training distinguishes objects. Learning a new object takes about 20 minutes, including a handful of scenes; optimization runs 3500 steps in about 13 minutes on one 1080 Ti or Titan Xp, and a static-scene scan takes about 70 seconds. The setup uses a calibrated Kuka IIWA LBR, a wrist-mounted Primesense Carmine 1.09 and a Schunk two-finger gripper, and the gripper's 6-DoF orientation needs further information . Dex-Net 2.0 scores parallel-jaw grasp candidates. It trains on 6.7 million synthetic datapoints from 1500 object models, each pairing a grasp-aligned depth crop with an analytic robust-epsilon quality label. The planner ranks antipodal candidates, checks reachability and table collision, and works on single-view depth of an isolated object on a planar worksurface, assuming rigid objects and known camera intrinsics. Missing depth on thin parts and collisions remain failure modes, and its pile demonstration separates objects before grasping . ## 6-DoF pose estimation, and how to read a claim about it Pose estimation turns a mask into a rigid body with a position and orientation, and methods divide by what they assume about the object. Instance-level methods train on specific objects. PoseCNN localizes each object's centre, predicts its distance and regresses a rotation quaternion with a loss that handles symmetric objects. It introduced YCB-Video, 21 objects across 92 videos and 133,827 frames . DOPE, trained only on synthetic domain-randomized and photorealistic data, performs competitively with a network trained on real and synthetic data . Category-level methods such as NOCS estimate the pose and size of unseen instances in known categories with no exact CAD model at training or test time . Novel-object methods drop per-object training. MegaPose uses render-and-compare against a CAD model supplied at test time . FoundationPose works from a CAD model or a few reference images and reports results comparable to instance-level methods . SAM-6D builds proposals with SAM, then treats pose as partial-to-partial point matching on cluttered RGB-D images . Any6D needs one RGB-D anchor image to estimate both the 6D pose and size of an unknown object . SAM 3D predicts geometry, texture and layout from one image and reports at least a 5:1 win rate in human preference tests . To read a pose result, check its evaluation protocol. Hinterstoisser and colleagues evaluate a model $\mathcal M$ with ground-truth pose $(R,T)$ and estimate $(\tilde R,\tilde T)$ by averaging distances between corresponding transformed model points
: $$ m = \operatorname{avg}_{x \in \mathcal M} \lVert (Rx+T)-(\tilde R x+\tilde T) \rVert $$ An estimate is correct when $m \leq k_m d$, where $d$ is the model's diameter and $k_m$ a chosen coefficient; their LINEMOD evaluation uses $k_m=0.1$
. For the symmetry-aware pose error, each ground-truth-transformed point is matched to its nearest estimated-pose point before averaging
: $$ m = \operatorname{avg}_{x_1 \in \mathcal M} \min_{x_2 \in \mathcal M} \lVert (Rx_1+T)-(\tilde R x_2+\tilde T) \rVert $$ They apply this rule to objects that are ambiguous, or look ambiguous from some views, naming "cup", "bowl", "box" and "glue"
. The BOP Challenge 2023 report scores 6-DoF localization differently. Each dataset score averages the VSD, MSSD and MSPD recalls, each over several thresholds with a strict test $e < \theta_e$, and $AR_C$ averages seven core datasets (LM-O, T-LESS, ITODD, HB, YCB-V, TUD-L, IC-BIN) on a 0 to 100 scale. VSD uses the visible surface, while MSSD and MSPD use pre-identified symmetries. Seen and unseen tracks share the method, with object identities and instance counts supplied at test time. Its 2D-detection $AP_C$ averages over objects first
. The 2020 report, which supplies the threshold grids, marks where deep-network methods caught up with the point-pair-feature methods that had dominated earlier editions . From 2017 to 2023, seen-object accuracy rose from 56.9 to 85.6 $AR_C$, a relative gain of over 50 percent. The endpoints are Vidal's point-pair-feature method with ICP and no training images, and GPose2023 with object-specific networks trained on PBR and real images
. For unseen objects, GenFlow-MultiHypo16 led 2023's Task 4 with 67.4 $AR_C$, against 69.8 for the best 2020 seen-object entry, CosyPose, and the report calls these comparable across distinct tracks. Their average image times were 34.58 and 13.74 seconds on unmatched hardware. GenFlow uses one network across datasets with CNOS-fastSAM detections and recurrent-flow refinement, while CosyPose uses dataset-specific networks with DeepIM and ICP refinement. Task 4 still supplies mesh models for onboarding, capped at 5 minutes per object on one GPU with no real images of the objects, and GenFlow still fails under heavy occlusion
. CosyPose refines cameras and object poses jointly by object-level bundle adjustment over all views . The BOP 2024 report moved the frontier. Its best unseen-object method, FreeZeV2.1, is 22% more accurate on BOP-Classic-Core than GenFlow and 4% behind GPose2023, at 24.9 versus 2.7 seconds per image. Co-op takes 0.8 seconds per image and is 13% more accurate than GenFlow. The 2024 edition added model-free tasks onboarded from reference videos, and the report names 2D detection as the main bottleneck for unseen objects . ## Visual servoing: image-based and position-based control Visual servoing uses vision inside the control loop. Hutchinson, Hager and Corke's 1996 tutorial divides such systems into position-based and image-based classes . Espiau, Chaumette and Rives's 1992 paper applies a task-function framework to image-based control, with a task function designed for regulation that need not be the raw feature difference. Its interaction matrix relates feature rates to the camera's translational and rotational velocity in the camera frame. Convergence depends on task and model conditions, and neglecting target motion can leave a tracking error . For a fixed goal and motionless target, Chaumette and Hutchinson's Part I writes $\dot{s} = L_s v_c$, with $v_c$ the camera's six-component spatial velocity. Image-based visual servoing (IBVS) uses image features, and position-based visual servoing (PBVS) uses estimated pose. The IBVS point-feature interaction matrix still uses depth and camera intrinsics, estimated from current depths or depths at the desired pose
. Redundant-feature IBVS is locally asymptotically stable when the interaction matrices have full rank and the estimated pseudoinverse times the true matrix meets a positivity condition. Coarse estimates can change the camera path without changing the final pose, while poor ones can make the system unstable. Large displacements can meet local minima or singularities, and PBVS points can leave the field of view. In PBVS, pose-estimation errors affect final accuracy
. Part II (2007) covers interaction-matrix estimation, hybrid and partitioned control, optimization, switching, trajectory planning and target tracking. Its switching and planning methods address visibility, occlusions and joint limits, and its joint-space formulations cover eye-in-hand and eye-to-hand systems
. Bateux and colleagues fine-tuned a CNN to estimate the relative pose between current and desired images and kept a pose-based control law . Learned servoing can also aim the camera. EyeRobot 2.0, from Ken Goldberg (UC Berkeley) and colleagues (October 2026), swivels the two eye viewpoints of a single stereo camera to fixate a 3D point. A gaze-servoing policy and a fixation selector are both trained with RL on real data. Without wrist cameras, a standard policy on passive stereo fell from 52% to 27% real-world success. EyeRobot 2.0 beat passive stereo by 40% in real trials and, when a grasped object hid the wrist views, more than doubled the success of policies that had them, 48% against 22% . ## Separate model error from geometric error Hand-eye accuracy depends on noise and motion range, so Enebuse and colleagues advise considering those conditions when benchmarking or calibrating . A detector can keep stable image coordinates while the robot misses because the camera transform drifted, and a depth model can improve pixel metrics while grasps fail because invalid values cluster on the target material. Each stage is evaluated in its native output before the geometry that consumes it. The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) defines the geometric checks, rerun after camera remounts, lens changes, time-source changes and resizing updates. The [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) shows where images, transforms and timestamps meet at runtime. ## What the end-to-end models replaced End-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) policies absorb the explicit pipeline into weights. Gemini Robotics is a VLA model that controls robots directly, built on an embodied-reasoning model whose capabilities include object detection, pointing, trajectory and grasp prediction, multi-view correspondence and 3D bounding boxes . Such a policy needs no detector class or CAD model for a new object. It also has no hand-eye residual to re-solve when it misses a grasp by 8 mm. Explicit geometric intermediates persist in some frontier systems. The [keypoint interfaces](/manipulation/hierarchical) kept geometry explicit while a learned model produced it. MolmoAct encodes observations into depth-aware perception tokens and generates editable trajectory traces before predicting low-level actions . Google DeepMind reports that Gemini Robotics-ER 1.6 improves pointing, counting and success detection, and acts as a robot's high-level reasoning model that calls VLAs as tools .

edits.before:
ROS 2 is the integration layer around a robot policy. It carries sensor streams, coordinate transforms, commands, task requests, logs and lifecycle state between processes. It is not an operating system and it is not the controller itself. For a machine-learning engineer, the shortest useful mental model is a typed, distributed dataflow graph with explicit delivery policies and a shared transform tree.

As of August 2026, Lyrical Luth is the current ROS 2 long-term-support release, released in May 2026 and supported through May 2031 <Cite id="ros2-lyrical-2026" />. Choose a supported stable distribution for a product; use Rolling only when contributing to the next release.

Try the check below and choose the ROS interface that matches a long-running robot task with feedback and cancellation.
edits.after: ROS 2 is the second generation of the Robot Operating System, a modular framework of freely available robot software, rebuilt from the ground up because ROS 1 lacked production-grade features <Cite id="ros2-science-robotics-2022" />. Lyrical Luth, the current long-term-support release, shipped on 22 May 2026 and is supported until May 2031 <Cite id="ros2-lyrical-2026" /> <Cite id="ros2-distributions-2026" />.

A node is one participant in the graph, such as a camera driver, policy server or controller bridge. Nodes talk through topics for continuous streams, services for short request-response calls, and actions for long-running goals with feedback, cancellation and a result <Cite id="ros2-interfaces-2026" />. ROS-LLM attaches language-model agents through the same actions and services <Cite id="ros-llm-2024" />. A `geometry_msgs/PoseStamped` carries the timestamp and frame identifier that a bare array lacks. REP 103 standardizes ROS on SI units <Cite id="rep-103-2010" />.

edits.before: Quality of Service controls delivery behavior. Reliability, durability, history, depth, deadline and lifespan can change which messages arrive and how old they are. ROS 2's sensor-data profile favors timely latest samples with best-effort reliability, while the default profile is reliable with a deeper queue <Cite id="ros2-qos-2026" />.
edits.after: ROS 2 inherits Quality of Service (QoS) from DDS, which exposes reliability and related parameters to control communication <Cite id="ros2-dds-design-2014" />. The default profile keeps the last 10 messages and delivers reliably; the sensor-data profile uses best effort and a smaller queue, because timely readings matter more than complete ones <Cite id="ros2-qos-2026" />. Lifespan silently drops messages older than its limit, and endpoints with incompatible policies never connect <Cite id="ros2-qos-2026" />.

edits.before:
For policy inference, stale data is often worse than a dropped frame. A reliable camera subscription with a large queue can deliver every image and make the policy act on the past. A best-effort queue of one may be the correct contract on a local robot network. State and command channels may need different choices.

Publisher and subscriber QoS must be compatible or they will not connect. Treat a silent topic as a possible QoS mismatch before debugging the neural code.

Record message age at the policy boundary. The tensor may have the right shape while the physical state it describes is already obsolete.
edits.after: A reliable camera subscription with a deep queue can make a policy act on old images, so log message age at the policy boundary. End-to-end latency depends strongly on the DDS implementation, and ROS 2 can add 50% over raw DDS <Cite id="ros2-latency-2021" />. Since Kilted Kaiju (May 2025), Zenoh's `rmw_zenoh_cpp` is a Tier 1 middleware <Cite id="ros2-kilted-2025" />.

edits.before:
Every observation used together should refer to a defensible time. Camera, depth, joint state and force streams arrive at different rates and latencies. Use acquisition timestamps alongside arrival times. Decide whether to use exact synchronization, approximate synchronization or interpolation of the robot state to the image timestamp.

Separate three clocks in logs: source timestamp, receipt timestamp and inference completion. Then you can decompose latency into sensing, transport, preprocessing, model execution and command delivery.

Simulation introduces ROS time, where `/clock` can advance faster, slower or discontinuously relative to wall time. Nodes that mix the two will produce timeouts and derivative estimates that look like random instability.

The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) covers the spatial and temporal alignment needed before transitions become training examples.
edits.after: Camera, depth, joint and force streams arrive at different rates, so a policy's inputs need acquisition timestamps as well as arrival times. MCAP records both a publish time and a log time for every message <Cite id="mcap-spec-2026" />. Logging source, receipt and inference-completion times splits latency into sensing, transport, model execution and command delivery, and ros2_tracing instruments ROS 2 at an average overhead of 0.0033 ms per message <Cite id="ros2-tracing-2022" />. With `use_sim_time` set, ROS time follows the latest `/clock` message <Cite id="ros2-clock-design" />, so nodes that mix it with wall time see spurious timeouts. The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) covers spatial and temporal alignment.

edits.before: tf2 maintains time-indexed rigid transforms between frames such as `map`, `odom`, `base_link`, camera optical frames, wrist and tool. A transform lookup asks where one frame was relative to another at a particular time.
edits.after: tf2 keeps a time-buffered tree of coordinate frames, transforms data between any two frames at any time, and can broadcast static transforms that never change <Cite id="tf2-docs-2026" />. Its predecessor, tf, was built because frame bookkeeping was a common source of bugs <Cite id="tf-library-2013" />. A lookup at an image timestamp can wait for the transform; the tf2 tutorial raises an exception only if it is still unavailable after a 50 ms timeout <Cite id="tf2-time-tutorial-2026" />.

edits.before:
The tree should reflect ownership. Static transforms describe fixed mounting geometry. Dynamic transforms come from state estimation and joint state. Avoid publishing two authorities for the same edge. Name optical frames according to their axis convention rather than silently reusing a mechanical camera frame.

At the policy boundary, transform observations and actions deliberately. If training used base-frame <Term id="end-effector">end-effector</Term> deltas, deployment must not send tool-frame deltas with the same tensor layout. The geometry behind these transformations is developed in *Modern Robotics* <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />.
edits.after: REP 105 defines `odom` as a drifting short-term reference and `map` as a frame whose poses can jump <Cite id="rep-105-2010" />. Camera optical frames take an `_optical` suffix and a different axis convention <Cite id="rep-103-2010" />. If training used base-frame <Term id="end-effector">end-effector</Term> deltas, deployment cannot send tool-frame deltas in the same layout; *Modern Robotics* covers the geometry <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />.

URDF, the most common robot-description format <Cite id="urdf-dataset-2023" />, lists links, joints, geometry and limits, and `robot_state_publisher` combines it with joint states to publish the frame tree. MoveIt 2's Planning Scene combines robot state, robot model and world geometry for forward and inverse kinematics, constraint checks and collision checking <Cite id="moveit-planning-scene-2026" />. A learned policy can use it to plan a collision-free approach, reject waypoints in collision, or provide a classical baseline.

edits.before:
rosbag2 records topic messages with timestamps for replay. It is invaluable for debugging and dataset capture, but a bag is not automatically a machine-learning dataset.

Record the raw sensor topics, transforms, joint state, commands, controller state, task events, software version and calibration identity. Preserve QoS information and verify that high-bandwidth topics were actually recorded. Replay a small bag through preprocessing in continuous integration so schema drift fails early.

Convert bags into immutable training shards with a versioned transformation. Keep the bag URI and message timestamps in provenance so a suspicious sample can be traced back to raw traffic as well as its tensor file.
edits.after: rosbag2 records timestamped messages for replay, in MCAP by default since Iron Irwini <Cite id="ros2-iron-mcap-2023" />. Since Kilted, `ros2 bag play --message-order sent` replays in publication order instead of the default receipt order <Cite id="ros2-kilted-2025" />. A bag is a raw record. Learning pipelines convert it to episode formats such as RLDS, a standard lossless format <Cite id="rlds-2021" />.

edits.before: A robust learned-policy graph often has six nodes or components:
edits.after: One robust layout for a learned-policy graph separates drivers, state assembly, a policy server, a command gate, a controller bridge and a supervisor. The supervisor can drive ROS 2 managed nodes, which leave a primary state only at an external supervisor's request or on an error in the Active state <Cite id="ros2-lifecycle-design-2015" />. Inference stays outside the hard real-time loop unless its worst case fits; ROS 2's real-time guidance keeps page faults, dynamic allocation and indefinitely blocking synchronization out of that path <Cite id="ros2-realtime-docs-2026" />. Lyrical's EventsCBGExecutor cuts executor CPU overhead, but its event queue is unbounded <Cite id="ros2-executors-2026" />.

Lyrical's `rosidl::Buffer` lets a `uint8[]` field live in GPU memory without changing the .msg file <Cite id="ros2-buffer-backends-2026" />. NVIDIA deprecated its NITROS transport on 21 September 2026 in favor of `rosidl::Buffer` with a CUDA backend <Cite id="isaac-ros-nitros-2026" />, noting that host round-trips add latency and consume CPU and memory bandwidth <Cite id="isaac-ros-rosidl-buffer-2026" />.

edits.before:
Nav2 is the reference ROS 2 navigation stack and applies a similar split: global planning over a map, local control against current obstacles, behavior coordination and recovery <Cite id="nav2-2020" />. Learned components can work within this graph.

A learned local controller can consume the same costmap and goal interface as a classical one. That preserves test harnesses and fallback behavior. The [scene-representation module](/classical/scene-representation) explains why planning, rendering and learning can call for different representations of the map.
edits.after: Nav2 uses a behavior tree to orchestrate planner, controller and recovery servers <Cite id="nav2-2020" />. Its standard planner, Smac Planner, powers thousands of robots, its authors report <Cite id="smac-planner-2024" />. Costmap 2D accepts sensor-processing plugins for AI outputs and semantic information <Cite id="nav2-costmap-2d-2026" />, so a learned local controller can consume the same costmap and goal interface as a classical one and keep its test harness and fallback. The [scene-representation module](/classical/scene-representation) explains the map choices.

edits.before:
- **Correct tensor, wrong frame:** training and deployment disagree about base, tool or camera coordinates.
- **Reliable but stale:** a queue preserves old images and hides latency.
- **Two command publishers:** teleoperation and policy both control the same interface without arbitration.
- **Bag without transforms:** images and joints were recorded but cannot be reconstructed in a common frame.
- **Simulation-only time assumptions:** a node uses wall time and breaks under `/clock`.
- **One giant node:** drivers, inference and hardware commands share a failure domain and cannot be replayed independently.

The remedy is explicit contracts. Topics carry timestamped state, tf2 carries geometry, QoS carries delivery intent, and the controller bridge carries action semantics. The learned model is then replaceable without rewriting the robot around it, which is the production property ROS 2 should provide.
edits.after: Frequent failures are a policy deployed in a different frame from its training data, a reliable queue that hides latency, and two command publishers without arbitration. Others are bags without transforms, wall-time assumptions under `/clock`, and one node holding drivers, inference and hardware commands. DDS implementations are compatible only in limited circumstances, so a system should use one ROS version and one RMW implementation <Cite id="ros2-middleware-vendors-2026" />. Nodes are not guaranteed to communicate across distributions; Jazzy is supported until May 2029 and Humble until May 2027 <Cite id="ros2-distributions-2026" />. ROS 1 ended when Noetic reached end of life in May 2025 <Cite id="noetic-eol-2025" />.
