import { SceneRepresentationLadder } from '@/components/interactive/scene-representation-ladder';

Scene representation is what a robot keeps in memory about the space around it, in a form it can query. [Perception](/classical/perception) answers where an object is right now. This module answers the other question a robot needs settled before it can move: what does it remember about the space it is standing in, and what can it ask of that memory.

The answers form a ladder. Each rung stores something different, and the choice is not a matter of fidelity, because a rung that draws the scene beautifully may be unable to answer the one question a planner needs.

## The ladder, and what each rung can answer

Three questions separate the rungs. Can the map say whether a given cell is free, so a planner can route through it. Can it supply a surface normal, so a contact solver knows which way the surface faces. Can it render the scene from a viewpoint the sensor never occupied. No representation on this ladder answers all three well; the differences follow from what each one stores.

Switch the representation selector below from the occupancy grid to the Gaussian splat and watch what happens to the region behind the occluder, which no sensor ray ever reached. Then move the resolution slider and notice what does not change.

<SceneRepresentationLadder className="my-6" />

The occupancy grid holds that region as an explicit unknown. The splat fills it with plausible geometry, rendered at the same confidence as the surfaces that were actually measured. Nothing in the splat's store distinguishes the two, and that single difference is the reason the rest of this module is worth reading.

### Point clouds and occupancy grids

A <Term id="point-cloud">point cloud</Term> is an unordered set of 3D points. PointNet treats its input this way and requires invariance to the order in which those points are supplied <Cite id="pointnet-2017" />. Its weakness is silence. A region with no points might be empty or might be unobserved, and the store cannot tell you which.

Moravec and Elfes projected wide-angle sonar measurements onto a two-dimensional horizontal <Term id="occupancy-grid">occupancy grid</Term>, combining readings from different sensors and robot positions. Each reading represented a probably empty beam interior and uncertainty about the reflecting point somewhere near the measured range. Overlapping readings refined these constraints <Cite id="moravec-elfes-1985" />. In their sonar map, a cell with no information is unknown. Zero represents unknown occupancy; negative and positive cell values represent probably empty and probably occupied regions, respectively <Cite id="moravec-elfes-1985" />.

### Signed-distance fields

Curless and Levoy replaced the occupancy value with a distance. Their volumetric method fuses range images into a cumulative weighted <Term id="signed-distance-field">signed distance function</Term>, from which the surface is recovered as the zero crossing <Cite id="curless-levoy-1996" />. The sign convention must be named. KinectFusion describes positive values toward visible free space and negative values on the non-visible side <Cite id="kinectfusion-2011" />. Curless and Levoy's hole-filling construction instead encodes empty space with negative $D_{min}$ and unseen space with positive $D_{max}$, both at zero weight <Cite id="curless-levoy-1996" />.

KinectFusion's author-hosted paper describes a Kinect supplying 11-bit, 640×480 depth frames at 30 Hz. Its coarse-to-fine ICP tracks the live depth frame against the fused global model; the commodity-GPU implementation tracks and maps at the sensor frame rate. A large planar scene filling most of the field of view can cause tracking drift or failure <Cite id="kinectfusion-2011" />.

Curless and Levoy truncate the distance ramps and weights near observed range points <Cite id="curless-levoy-1996" />. KinectFusion uses a projective TSDF: visible-space values beyond the truncation distance $\mu$ are capped at $\mu$, while non-visible points farther than $\mu$ from the surface are not measured <Cite id="kinectfusion-2011" />. KinectFusion distinguishes its projective TSDF from a true discrete signed-distance field. Its projective measurement is correct exactly at the surface or for an isolated point measurement; fusion produces an approximate pseudo-Euclidean distance metric. Near the zero level set, the method assumes the field gradient is orthogonal to the surface and estimates normals using numerical derivatives. Surface prediction marches along each ray to a zero crossing, then approximates the intersection using trilinearly interpolated field values <Cite id="kinectfusion-2011" />.

### Meshes, and then neural fields

A mesh adds connectivity, which buys a normal per face and a renderable surface, and costs you a hole wherever nothing was observed. Filling that hole invents geometry, which is fine for a rendering and a problem for a gripper.

NeRF fits a separate radiance field to a static scene. Its MLP predicts density from position and colour from position and viewing direction. Classical volume rendering accumulates those predictions along camera rays, and differentiability lets image error drive optimisation. The inputs include RGB photographs, camera poses, intrinsics and scene bounds; differentiability is not a guarantee that the recovered geometry is correct <Cite id="nerf-2020" />. The <Term id="neural-radiance-field">neural radiance field</Term> line then bought three separate things in three steps.

The original result demonstrated view-synthesis quality. Instant NGP then lowered optimisation cost by combining a trainable multiresolution hash encoding, smaller networks and fully fused CUDA kernels. Its NeRF model still learns from posed RGB images through a differentiable ray marcher; the speedup comes from the combined system. Rendering settings matter too: the paper reports a modular-synthesizer image accumulated over 128 samples in 5 seconds at 1080p on one RTX 3090, and a separate large natural 360-degree scene running at 10 frames per second on the same GPU. These are rendering settings, with no robot reconstruction or control rate measured <Cite id="instant-ngp-2022" />. <Term id="gaussian-splatting">3D Gaussian splatting</Term> brought rasterisation without a neural network in the rendering loop. It optimises Gaussian positions, anisotropic covariances, opacities and spherical-harmonic appearance from static-scene photographs with calibrated cameras. It projects the Gaussians to the image plane and alpha-blends sorted splats. The paper evaluates novel-view quality and rendering speed on established datasets using an A6000 GPU. Its abstract reports real-time rendering at 1080p, while the evaluation retains each dataset's native image resolution; these settings do not form a fixed-resolution benchmark <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />.

DUSt3R's network predicts dense pointmaps from a pair of RGB images without camera intrinsics or poses supplied at inference. The pointmaps share the first image's coordinate frame and have an unknown scale. The network is trained with geometric supervision and starts from pretrained CroCo weights. For an image collection, the pipeline then optimises the alignment of pairwise pointmaps in 3D; the feed-forward pairwise prediction is not an optimisation-free multiview reconstruction <Cite id="dust3r-2024" />.

MASt3R extends the same network with a dense local-feature head so matching is grounded in the same 3D prediction <Cite id="mast3r-2024" />.

## A radiance field is geometry for rendering

This wiki has already staked out the verdict, in the [world-models taxonomy](/world-models/taxonomy): a splat reconstruction is a learned renderer, so appearance is learned and physics is not, and a renderer alone has no answer to what happens under an action. The same conclusion follows from the other direction here. In the original 3DGS model, learned opacity participates in image-space alpha compositing; it is not a calibrated free/occupied/unknown cell classification. The stored primitive is a volumetric Gaussian, not an explicit triangle surface carrying contact normals. That does not make surface extraction impossible: the paper explicitly leaves mesh reconstruction as future work <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />.

SplatSim uses splats for rendering while PyBullet supplies the physics. The authors report zero-shot real-world transfer of diffusion policies trained on simulated demonstrations in four tasks using a UR5 and Robotiq 2F-85 gripper. Scene preparation includes manual robot segmentation, CAD-derived link bounds and ICP alignment. The paper lists RGB observations plus end-effector position and orientation as policy inputs in its diagram, while its test-time description specifies solely RGB. Both descriptions appear in the paper. Its experiments concern rigid-body manipulation <Cite id="splatsim-2024" />.

RoboGSim combines a Gaussian Reconstructor, Digital Twins Builder, Scene Composer and Interactive Engine. Multi-view images and supplied robot MDH parameters feed reconstruction; mesh assets and measured layout alignment connect the reconstruction to Isaac Sim. In its closed-loop evaluator, a policy acts on splat-rendered images, Isaac Sim handles inverse kinematics and physical interactions, and the resulting state drives the next rendering <Cite id="robogsim-2024" />. Novel-view augmentation, and scene memory. A rendering representation alone does not specify a contact model; geometric conversion and contact modelling are separate requirements.

Dex-NeRF uses a radiance field to render transparency-aware depth from view-independent learned density, then feeds that depth to a grasp planner. In their RealSense comparison, the camera failed to compute depth for most transparent objects in the tested scenes <Cite id="dex-nerf-2021" />. The planner uses the field's depth map.

OccWorld predicts how a 3D occupancy grid evolves and gets competitive planning results without instance or map supervision <Cite id="occworld-2023" />. Its occupancy prediction gives the planner a representation it can act on.

## SLAM: the system that builds the map

Every representation above assumes somebody produced it, from sensor data, while the robot was moving and did not know precisely where it was. That is simultaneous localisation and mapping, and [state estimation](/classical/state-estimation) supplies its machinery without ever assembling the system.

Cadena and colleagues separate a sensor-dependent front end, which abstracts measurements into models suitable for estimation and associates observations with state variables, from a back end that performs inference on those abstractions. The back end can feed information back to support loop-closure detection and validation <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

Front ends divide into feature-based and direct. A feature-based front end detects repeatable keypoints, describes them, and matches descriptors between frames; the 2015 monocular ORB-SLAM system uses ORB features for tracking, local mapping, relocalisation and loop closing. Tracking matches features and refines camera pose; mapping triangulates matched ORB features and runs local bundle adjustment. A DBoW2 vocabulary built from ORB descriptors supplies relocalisation and loop candidates, which require geometric validation <Cite id="orb-slam-2015" />.

ORB-SLAM3 supports visual SLAM with monocular, stereo and RGB-D inputs, and monocular-inertial and stereo-inertial SLAM with pinhole or fisheye cameras. Its IMU initialization uses MAP estimation and refinement. Tracking loss first triggers recovery attempts; persistent loss can start a new active map, while early loss after inertial initialization can discard an immature map. A revisit can trigger map merging only after place-recognition candidates pass geometric and covisibility checks; mature visual-inertial maps also undergo gravity-direction checks. Low texture remains a failure case, and slow motion can leave inertial initialization poorly constrained. <Cite id="orb-slam3-2021" />

A direct front end skips the detector entirely and optimises photometric error over sampled pixels jointly with the geometry, which is Direct Sparse Odometry's formulation <Cite id="dso-2018" />. The trade is legible: features are robust to brightness change and throw away most of the image, while direct methods use weakly textured regions a detector would ignore, and gain accuracy and robustness from a calibration of the camera's exposure, vignetting and response.

Cadena and colleagues describe odometric drift and explain that revisiting mapped landmarks can reduce and possibly correct trajectory drift; they also distinguish wheel odometry from lower-drift visual-inertial methods <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. In monocular ORB-SLAM, <Term id="loop-closure">loop closure</Term> requires geometric validation, then uses similarity alignment and Essential Graph optimization to distribute loop-closing error along the graph <Cite id="orb-slam-2015" />. This is not a guarantee that every revisit removes all error. For visual navigation, <Term id="place-recognition">place recognition</Term> asks whether the current image matches a place already stored in the map; Lowry and colleagues note that motion information can also inform this belief. Viewpoint, illumination and seasonal changes can alter the same place’s appearance, while different places can look alike (perceptual aliasing) <Cite id="lowry-2016-place-recognition" />.

In Cadena and colleagues' robustness argument, perceptual aliasing can produce false-positive data associations that lead to wrong back-end estimates; false negatives instead discard useful measurements and reduce estimation accuracy. Robust losses and loop-closure validation can mitigate outliers, but the survey describes remaining failures that depend on initialization and subsequent outlier rejection. This is not a universal ranking of the cost of every false match against every missed match. <Cite id="cadena-2016" />

The back end is where the smoothing formulations from [state estimation](/classical/state-estimation) do their work. Square Root SAM jointly estimates the trajectory and landmark map by maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference. Under Gaussian process and measurement models with known data associations, this becomes a nonlinear least-squares problem. With the reference frame fixed, nonlinear optimisation solves successive sparse linearised systems using QR of the measurement Jacobian or Cholesky of the information matrix; variable ordering controls fill-in <Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />. iSAM2 uses a Bayes tree for incremental reordering and relinearisation: it re-eliminates affected cliques and their ancestors, then reattaches unaffected subtrees. Thresholded state updates trade some accuracy for speed, and large loop closures can cost as much as a batch solve <Cite id="kaess-2012" />. Loop closure is precisely why smoothing displaced filtering here: relinearising the past is only possible if the past is still in the graph.

Cadena and colleagues describe sparse landmark maps built from discriminative features and dense geometric models better suited to obstacle avoidance and planning; dense models also appear in visual SLAM. They assess representations by storage size, construction cost and usefulness for the task, and describe more efficient volumetric storage schemes such as octrees and voxel hashing <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

Sensor choice depends on the sensor-environment pair: Cadena and colleagues note that two rooms may look identical to a 2D laser scanner yet be distinguishable by appearance to a camera. Severe illumination changes defeat the bag-of-words methods discussed in the review, while active range cameras can work in dark, untextured scenes but face range and external-light limitations <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

iMAP learns a scene-specific MLP from scratch from a handheld RGB-D stream, without prior training data. The network maps 3D coordinates to colour and volume density; rendering uses camera intrinsics. Tracking optimises the current camera pose against a fixed network, while mapping updates the network and selected keyframe poses. The MLP is the dense scene map, not the system's only stored data: RGB-D keyframes and poses are retained for replay, and network snapshots guide keyframe selection. The paper reports tracking at 10 Hz and mapping at 2 Hz on a single desktop CPU/GPU system. Live operation drops images arriving between processed frames; fine map detail takes minutes to develop. The demonstrated scope is room-scale mapping, and meshes are extracted for evaluation and visualisation rather than used by SLAM <Cite id="imap-2021" />.

NICE-SLAM uses hierarchical feature grids with three fixed, pretrained geometry decoders for coarse-, mid- and fine-scale occupancy, plus a separate colour grid and a colour decoder optimised online. The geometry decoders are pretrained using ConvONet's Synthetic Indoor Scene Dataset; scene grids are then optimised from RGB-D observations, with camera intrinsics used for rendering. Tracking estimates the current camera pose; the static-scene mapping formulation performs local bundle adjustment over scene features, the colour decoder and selected keyframe poses. The paper demonstrates reconstruction of a self-captured multi-room apartment, rather than unlimited scene scale. Geometric updates are local, but a global keyframe list is retained, colour can suffer forgetting and remain consistent only locally, and the system does not perform loop closure. Its reported 47 ms tracking and 130 ms mapping timings use 200 tracking pixels and 1,000 mapping pixels on an RTX 3090/Intel i7-10700K desktop. The large-scene experiments use higher sample counts, so those timings are not a latency guarantee for the apartment <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />.

## The deployed answer: costmaps and two planners

Navigation2 provides one concrete mobile-robot implementation of this pipeline. The map a navigation stack plans over is a <Term id="costmap">costmap</Term>: occupancy from the map and the live sensors, inflated by the robot's footprint, marked up with whatever else should influence the route. Lu, Hershberger and Smart proposed and implemented layered costmaps in the ROS Navigation stack. The method keeps an ordered list of semantically separate layers and accumulates their data into a master 2D costmap for path planning. Each update first gathers the layers' update bounds, then lets each layer update the master grid within those bounds. Some layers keep private grids, while others operate directly on the master; separating static-map and sensed-obstacle data does not prohibit overwriting static-map costs, which remains configurable <Cite id="layered-costmaps-2014" />. Navigation2 uses a layered costmap <Cite id="nav2-2020" />.

Navigation2 separates global planning from local control: the global planner computes a shortest route to a goal, while the controller uses local information to compute a local path and control signals. The two are plugins delegated to task-specific asynchronous servers. Navigation2, built on ROS 2, is the implementation used as the example here <Cite id="nav2-2020" />. The algorithms inside both are the ones in [motion planning](/classical/motion-planning), applied to a 2D grid instead of a robot arm's configuration space.

The deployed stack uses a representation that can answer the planner's question: whether a cell is free.

## A representation is a service contract

Choose a scene representation by the queries its consumers issue. Localization needs stable landmarks and uncertainty. Collision checking needs occupied volume, resolution and a conservative update rule. Grasping may need surface pose and object identity. Rendering needs view-dependent appearance. One representation can support several queries, but no reconstruction should be promoted merely because it looks complete.

For deployment, publish the frame, timestamp, resolution, confidence or unknown-state convention, update rate and invalidation rule with the map. Test that attached objects and removed obstacles propagate to the planning view before motion begins. The [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) describes this handoff through transforms and planning-scene updates. The distinction from a learned world model is equally important: a scene representation answers what is present now, while a world model must answer how the state changes under an action. The [simulator comparison](/world-models/world-models-vs-simulators) makes that boundary explicit.

import { SceneRepresentationLadder } from '@/components/interactive/scene-representation-ladder';

Scene representation is the form in which a robot stores what it knows about its surroundings so that planners, controllers and other consumers can query it <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Representations range from point clouds and occupancy grids to signed-distance fields, meshes and neural fields such as radiance fields and Gaussian splats <Cite id="cadena-2016" /><Cite id="neural-fields-survey-2024" />.

## The ladder, and what each rung can answer

Three queries separate the rungs: whether a cell is free for a planner, which way a surface faces for a contact solver, and what the scene looks like from a viewpoint the sensor never occupied. Cadena and colleagues judge representations by storage size, construction cost and usefulness for the task <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

<SceneRepresentationLadder className="my-6" />

An occupancy map can hold an occluded region as explicitly unknown, as OctoMap does for free and unknown space alongside occupied space <Cite id="octomap-2013" />. Learned reconstructors fill such regions instead: CUT3R can infer unseen regions of a scene by probing virtual, unobserved views <Cite id="cut3r-2025" />.

### Point clouds and occupancy grids

A <Term id="point-cloud">point cloud</Term> is an unordered set of 3D points, and PointNet requires invariance to the order in which they arrive <Cite id="pointnet-2017" />. A region without points is either empty or unobserved, and the store cannot say which.

Moravec and Elfes projected wide-angle sonar readings from different sensors and robot positions onto a 2D <Term id="occupancy-grid">occupancy grid</Term>. Each reading marked a probably empty beam interior and an uncertain reflecting point near the measured range, and overlapping readings refined these constraints. Zero represented unknown occupancy, and negative and positive values probably empty and probably occupied cells <Cite id="moravec-elfes-1985" />. OctoMap carries the three states into 3D in a compressed octree <Cite id="octomap-2013" />.

### Signed-distance fields

Curless and Levoy fuse range images into a cumulative weighted <Term id="signed-distance-field">signed distance function</Term> and recover the surface at its zero crossing, truncating distance ramps and weights near observed points. Their hole-filling construction marks empty space with negative $D_{min}$ and unseen space with positive $D_{max}$, both at zero weight <Cite id="curless-levoy-1996" />. KinectFusion uses the opposite sign: positive toward visible free space and negative on the non-visible side <Cite id="kinectfusion-2011" />.

KinectFusion fused 11-bit, 640×480 Kinect depth frames at 30 Hz, tracking each frame against the global model by coarse-to-fine ICP and mapping at the sensor rate on a commodity GPU. A large plane filling most of the view can cause drift or tracking failure. Its projective TSDF caps visible-space values at the truncation distance $\mu$, leaves non-visible points beyond $\mu$ unmeasured and is exact at the surface, so fusion yields an approximate pseudo-Euclidean distance. Normals come from numerical derivatives near the zero level set, and ray marching finds surfaces by trilinear interpolation <Cite id="kinectfusion-2011" />.

Trajectory optimizers need obstacle distances. Voxblox builds TSDFs faster than OctoMap builds its maps, then derives Euclidean signed distance fields (ESDFs) from them incrementally, more accurately than from occupancy <Cite id="voxblox-2016" />. On GPUs, nvblox reports up to 177x faster surface reconstruction and 31x faster distance-field computation <Cite id="nvblox-2023" />. Voxel hashing stores surface data densely only where measurements are observed <Cite id="voxel-hashing-2013" />.

### Meshes, and then neural fields

A mesh adds connectivity, giving each face a normal and a renderable surface, but leaves holes where nothing was observed, and filling them invents geometry <Cite id="curless-levoy-1996" />.

NeRF fits a <Term id="neural-radiance-field">neural radiance field</Term> to a static scene from posed RGB photographs, intrinsics and scene bounds. Its MLP predicts density from position and colour from position and viewing direction, and differentiable volume rendering lets image error drive optimization <Cite id="nerf-2020" />. Without regularization, a radiance field can fit its training images perfectly "for an arbitrary incorrect geometry", and Zhang and colleagues show that NeRF's MLP structure helps avoid this shape-radiance ambiguity <Cite id="nerfpp-2020" />. Instant NGP cut optimization cost with a multiresolution hash encoding, smaller networks and fully fused CUDA kernels. It rendered one scene at 1080p in 5 seconds over 128 samples and a large 360-degree scene at 10 frames per second on one RTX 3090 <Cite id="instant-ngp-2022" />. <Term id="gaussian-splatting">3D Gaussian splatting</Term> optimizes Gaussian positions, anisotropic covariances, opacities and spherical-harmonic appearance from calibrated photographs, then rasterizes by alpha-blending sorted splats. It reports real-time 1080p rendering, with results on an A6000 GPU <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />. A 2024 survey of over 200 robotics papers covers four neural-field frameworks: occupancy networks, signed distance fields, radiance fields and splats <Cite id="neural-fields-survey-2024" />.

DUSt3R predicts dense pointmaps from a pair of RGB images without intrinsics or poses, in the first image's frame and at unknown scale, trained with geometric supervision from pretrained CroCo weights. For an image collection, it then optimizes the alignment of pairwise pointmaps in 3D <Cite id="dust3r-2024" />. MASt3R adds a dense local-feature head so matching rests on the same 3D prediction <Cite id="mast3r-2024" />. Feed-forward models now cover whole collections. VGGT infers cameras, point maps, depth maps and point tracks from one, a few or hundreds of views in under one second <Cite id="vggt-2025" />. MapAnything accepts optional intrinsics, poses or depth and regresses metric geometry and cameras <Cite id="mapanything-2025" />. π³ drops the reference view, an anchor its authors call a source of instability <Cite id="pi3-2025" />. Depth Anything 3 reports average camera pose accuracy 44.3% higher than VGGT <Cite id="depth-anything-3-2025" />.

## A radiance field is geometry for rendering

The [world-models taxonomy](/world-models/taxonomy) treats a splat reconstruction as a learned renderer: appearance is learned and physics is not. In the original 3DGS, learned opacity is an image-space alpha-compositing weight with no free, occupied or unknown label, and the stored primitive is a volumetric Gaussian <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />. The paper names mesh reconstruction as an open direction <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />. SuGaR then aligned Gaussians with surfaces and extracted meshes by Poisson reconstruction <Cite id="sugar-2023" />. 2D Gaussian Splatting collapses the volume into oriented planar disks for view-consistent geometry, since 3D Gaussians fail to represent surfaces accurately <Cite id="2dgs-2024" />.

Simulators pair splats for appearance with separate physics. SplatSim renders with splats while PyBullet supplies physics <Cite id="splatsim-2024" />. Its authors report zero-shot real-world transfer of diffusion policies on four rigid-body tasks with a UR5 and Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, after manual robot segmentation and ICP alignment <Cite id="splatsim-2024" />. In RoboGSim's closed-loop evaluator, a policy acts on splat-rendered images while Isaac Sim handles inverse kinematics and physical interaction, from multi-view images, supplied MDH parameters and mesh assets <Cite id="robogsim-2024" />. PhysTwin combines spring-mass simulation, generative shape models and Gaussian splats for deformable objects <Cite id="phystwin-2025" />.

Other fields serve a planner directly. Dex-NeRF renders transparency-aware depth from learned density for a grasp planner, where a RealSense camera failed to compute depth for most transparent objects tested <Cite id="dex-nerf-2021" />. Distilled feature fields add semantics from 2D foundation models to 3D geometry for language-guided 6-DoF grasping <Cite id="f3rm-2023" />. OccWorld predicts how a 3D occupancy grid evolves and plans competitively without instance or map supervision <Cite id="occworld-2023" />.

ParticleSplat, from Deepak Pathak (Carnegie Mellon) and colleagues (September 2026), encodes posed multi-view images into latent particles that decode to 3D Gaussians, trained with a novel-view synthesis objective. Object masks emerge without labels, moving a particle moves its object, and the representation improved downstream manipulation <Cite id="particlesplat-2026" />.

## SLAM: the system that builds the map

Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) builds such maps from sensor data while the robot moves without knowing its exact pose. Cadena and colleagues separate a sensor-dependent front end, which abstracts measurements and associates them with state variables, from a back end that performs inference and feeds information back for loop-closure detection and validation <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. [State estimation](/classical/state-estimation) covers the inference machinery.

Front ends are feature-based or direct. Monocular ORB-SLAM (2015) uses ORB features for tracking, local mapping, relocalization and loop closing, triangulating matched features and running local bundle adjustment. Its DBoW2 vocabulary proposes relocalization and loop candidates that need geometric validation <Cite id="orb-slam-2015" />. DBoW2's binary bag of words takes 22 ms per frame on a 26,300-image sequence <Cite id="dbow2-2012" />. ORB-SLAM3 supports stereo, RGB-D and visual-inertial modes with pinhole or fisheye cameras and MAP-based IMU initialization. It starts a new map after persistent tracking loss and merges maps only after geometric and covisibility checks, plus gravity-direction checks for mature visual-inertial maps. Low texture remains the main failure case, and slow motion can delay inertial initialization <Cite id="orb-slam3-2021" />.

Direct Sparse Odometry skips the detector and optimizes photometric error over sampled pixels jointly with geometry <Cite id="dso-2018" />. Features are robust to brightness change, while a direct method can sample any region with intensity gradient, including near-featureless walls, and gains from calibrating exposure, vignetting and camera response <Cite id="dso-2018" />. Learned systems keep classical machinery: DROID-SLAM iterates camera pose and per-pixel depth through a dense bundle-adjustment layer <Cite id="droid-slam-2021" />.

Revisiting mapped landmarks can reduce odometric drift and in some cases correct it, and visual-inertial methods drift less than wheel odometry <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Monocular ORB-SLAM validates a <Term id="loop-closure">loop closure</Term> geometrically, then spreads its error with similarity alignment and Essential Graph optimization <Cite id="orb-slam-2015" />. <Term id="place-recognition">Place recognition</Term> asks whether the current image matches a stored place, and motion information can also inform that belief. Viewpoint, illumination and seasonal changes alter one place's appearance, and different places can look alike, which is perceptual aliasing <Cite id="lowry-2016-place-recognition" />. AnyLoc builds place recognition on off-the-shelf self-supervised features, works from urban to underwater and subterranean settings without retraining, and reports up to 4x higher performance than prior approaches <Cite id="anyloc-2023" />.

Perceptual aliasing can create false-positive associations that corrupt back-end estimates, while false negatives discard useful measurements. Robust losses and loop-closure validation mitigate outliers, though failures remain that depend on initialization <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Graduated non-convexity solvers tolerate 70 to 80% outliers, without a guarantee of global optimality <Cite id="gnc-2019" />.

In the back end, Square Root SAM estimates the trajectory and landmark map jointly by MAP inference, which under Gaussian models with known data associations is sparse nonlinear least squares. It solves successive linearized systems by QR or Cholesky, and variable ordering controls fill-in <Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />. The iSAM2 method adds incremental reordering and relinearization on a Bayes tree. Thresholded updates trade some accuracy for speed, and a large loop closure can cost as much as a batch solve <Cite id="kaess-2012" />. Smoothing suits loop closure because relinearizing the past requires the past to stay in the graph. Cadena and colleagues contrast sparse landmark maps with dense models suited to obstacle avoidance, and cite octrees and voxel hashing as efficient volumetric storage. Two rooms can look identical to a 2D laser yet differ to a camera. Severe illumination changes defeat bag-of-words methods, and active range cameras work in dark, untextured scenes but face range and external-light limits <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

The iMAP system learns a scene-specific MLP from scratch at room scale from a handheld RGB-D stream. It tracks at 10 Hz and maps at 2 Hz on a desktop CPU and GPU, retaining keyframes for replay <Cite id="imap-2021" />. NICE-SLAM uses hierarchical feature grids with pretrained geometry decoders, reconstructs a multi-room apartment and performs no loop closure <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />. Its 47 ms tracking and 130 ms mapping times use small pixel samples on an RTX 3090 <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />. SplaTAM maps with 3D Gaussians from an RGB-D camera and uses a silhouette mask to determine whether areas were previously mapped <Cite id="splatam-2023" />. Gaussian Splatting SLAM runs monocular SLAM live at 3 fps with Gaussians as the only representation <Cite id="monogs-2023" />. Systems on learned 3D priors report higher frame rates: MASt3R-SLAM runs at 15 FPS with loop closure and second-order global optimization <Cite id="mast3r-slam-2024" />. SLAM3R reconstructs from monocular video at 20+ FPS without solving camera parameters <Cite id="slam3r-2024" />. VGGT-SLAM aligns submaps with 15-degree-of-freedom homographies, the projective ambiguity of uncalibrated cameras <Cite id="vggt-slam-2025" />.

## The deployed answer: costmaps and two planners

A navigation stack plans over a <Term id="costmap">costmap</Term>: occupancy from the map and live sensors, inflated by the robot's footprint. Lu, Hershberger and Smart's layered costmaps keep an ordered list of semantically separate layers and accumulate them into a master 2D costmap. Each update gathers the layers' bounds, then lets each layer write the master grid within them; a configuration setting decides whether sensed obstacles overwrite static-map costs <Cite id="layered-costmaps-2014" />. Cartographer, a 2D LIDAR SLAM system, maps and closes loops in real time at 5 cm resolution on a backpack platform <Cite id="cartographer-2016" />.

Navigation2, built on ROS 2, uses a layered costmap. Its global planner computes a shortest route to the goal, and a separate controller computes a local path and control signals, each a plugin in an asynchronous server <Cite id="nav2-2020" />. Its Smac Planner provides cost-aware A\*, Hybrid-A\* and State Lattice planners for Ackermann, legged and large non-circular robots <Cite id="smac-planner-2024" />. Its `track_unknown_space` option defaults to false, which treats unknown space as free; keeping the unknown state requires enabling it <Cite id="nav2-costmap-2d-2026" />. The planning algorithms are those of [motion planning](/classical/motion-planning) on a 2D grid.

## A representation is a service contract

[Perception](/classical/perception) locates objects in the current frame. Consumers issue different queries: localization needs stable landmarks, collision checking needs occupied volume and a conservative update rule, grasping needs surface pose and identity, and rendering needs appearance. Hydra stacks rungs in one real-time system, building a local ESDF, extracting a topological map of places from it and segmenting places into rooms <Cite id="hydra-2022" />. ConceptFusion fuses pixel-aligned open-set features into 3D maps through traditional SLAM <Cite id="conceptfusion-2023" />. ConceptGraphs builds open-vocabulary, graph-structured 3D scene representations because per-point feature maps do not scale well to larger environments <Cite id="conceptgraphs-2023" />.

SceneLM, from Jitendra Malik (UC Berkeley), Marco Pavone and colleagues (September 2026), keeps the whole map as a structured text list of objects that one vision-language model edits after each image. On language-grounded retrieval and localization benchmarks it performed competitively with complete mapping pipelines, with a map 6 to 12 times more compact, and it ran online on an edge device aboard a quadruped <Cite id="scenelm-2026" />.

A deployed map publishes its frame, timestamp, resolution, unknown-state convention, update rate and invalidation rule. In MoveIt 2, the planning scene holds the robot's current state, its model and the world representation for collision checking, and a monitor maintains it from parameters and topic subscriptions <Cite id="moveit-planning-scene-2026" />. Attached or removed objects must reach that view before motion; the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) covers transforms and the planning scene. A scene representation answers what is present now, while a world model must answer how state changes under an action, as the [simulator comparison](/world-models/world-models-vs-simulators) sets out.

State estimation is the discipline that turns a robot's stream of sensor readings into a usable estimate of its state, with an honest number attached describing how wrong the estimate might be. [Control](/classical/control) closes the loop under one quiet assumption: that someone knows the state. The pole's angle, the arm's configuration, the quadruped's velocity over ground. Nobody does. What the robot actually has is a stream of sensor readings, each one noisy, some biased, a few missing outright.

The honest number is what separates the field from curve fitting. A controller that knows the estimate's uncertainty can act cautiously when the number is large and aggressively when it is small; a controller handed a bare guess cannot. Every estimator in this module is built to carry both.

The scene below is that idea, one step at a time. A target wanders in one dimension and a position sensor drops about one reading in five; the scene holds one measured step of the seeded filter and walks it beat by beat: the prior belief as a dot with its two-sigma ellipse, the predict step smearing both along the motion model, the arriving reading with its own wider, position-only ellipse, and the update that fuses the two through the gain K. Try the Play button, or step through it with the arrow keys; the numbers in the readout are the filter's own.
edits.after: State estimation is the computation of a robot's state, such as its [configuration](/classical/kinematics) or velocity over ground, from noisy, biased and intermittent sensor readings. Probabilistic estimators report a belief, so each estimate carries its uncertainty <Cite id="thrun-2005" />. [Planning](/classical/motion-planning) and [control](/classical/control) assume that this state is known.

edits.before:
McGee and Schmidt's November 1985 NASA history credits Schmidt's Ames group with adapting Kalman's linear filter to nonlinear circumlunar navigation in the early 1960s. By early 1961, their simulations supported the approach, but operation on available flight computers had not yet been verified. The report distinguishes this work from Battin's Apollo navigation studies at MIT and Potter's square-root implementation used in Apollo. It also records the decision to use ground radar for primary Apollo navigation, with an onboard backup. This is the participants' retrospective account, not a claim that Ames alone engineered the flight system<br className="lg:hidden" /><Cite id="mcgee-schmidt-1985" />.

That is what the scene at the top of this module is showing. The belief is the dot with its two-sigma ellipse, the reading z is the cross with the wider, position-only ellipse, and the gain K is the point on the segment between the prediction and the reading. On the demonstrated step the filter weighs its prediction against the sensor at 0.62 to 0.38, so the posterior lands most of the way toward z, and the posterior ellipse comes out narrower than either parent: the one-sigma position uncertainty in the readout reads 0.94 before the predict, 1.27 after it, and 0.79 once z is fused. The world's noise is fixed by the seed named in the status line, and the filter's assumed noise is matched to it, which is why the gain lands where it does. Believing the sensor more shrinks the ellipse toward the reading; believing the motion model more leaves it drifting with the prediction.

One more thing to notice: the ellipse is a claim the filter makes about itself. Assume noise quieter than the world the filter actually lives in and it draws a narrow ellipse that the truth keeps escaping. An overconfident filter is worse than no filter, because nothing downstream knows to distrust it.

A single fusion is worth stepping through; a whole run is worth watching. The clip below plays the same seeded filter from step 0 to step 240, and the band tells the story: it widens across every dropout and tightens on every reading.
edits.after: McGee and Schmidt's 1985 NASA history credits Schmidt's Ames group with adapting the filter to nonlinear circumlunar navigation in the early 1960s. The report separates this work from Battin's Apollo studies at MIT and Potter's square-root implementation used in Apollo. Primary Apollo navigation used ground radar, with an onboard backup <Cite id="mcgee-schmidt-1985" />.

edits.before: Real robots are not linear. Joint angles enter through sines and cosines, range sensors see a nonlinear slice of the world, and the process model becomes $x_t = g(x_{t-1}, u_t) + w_t$ with measurements $z_t = h(x_t) + v_t$. The extended Kalman filter keeps the Gaussian belief and makes the recursion local: linearize both models about the current estimate using their <Term id="jacobian">Jacobians</Term> $G_t = \partial g / \partial x$ and $H_t = \partial h / \partial x$, then propagate the covariance through the tangent system <Cite id="thrun-2005" />:
edits.after: Real robots are nonlinear: joint angles enter through sines and cosines, so the models become $x_t = g(x_{t-1}, u_t) + w_t$ and $z_t = h(x_t) + v_t$. The extended Kalman filter keeps the Gaussian belief, linearizes both models about the current estimate with their <Term id="jacobian">Jacobians</Term> $G_t = \partial g / \partial x$ and $H_t = \partial h / \partial x$, and propagates the covariance through the tangent system <Cite id="thrun-2005" />:

edits.before: The mean moves through the true nonlinear maps $g$ and $h$; only the covariance takes the linearized route. In McGee and Schmidt's history, the Ames group moved from linearization about a nominal reference trajectory to relinearization about the *current estimated state*. They thought this "might offer substantial advantages". An accidentally off-nominal simulation converged after initial overshoots; the report calls this modification the extended Kalman filter. That example was not a general convergence guarantee: the report also discusses instability from round-off, inadequate statistical models and nonlinearities<br className="lg:hidden" /><Cite id="mcgee-schmidt-1985" />.
edits.after:
The mean moves through the true maps $g$ and $h$; only the covariance takes the linearized route <Cite id="thrun-2005" />. The Ames group moved from linearizing about a nominal reference trajectory to relinearizing about the *current estimated state*, which they hoped would bring "substantial advantages". An accidentally off-nominal simulation converged after initial overshoots, and the report names this modification the extended Kalman filter. It also discusses instability from round-off, inadequate statistical models and nonlinearities <Cite id="mcgee-schmidt-1985" />.

Linearization holds near the estimate, which is the uncertain quantity. Where the nonlinearity is strong over the region the covariance covers, $\Sigma$ stops describing the true error, and the filter grows overconfident and can diverge <Cite id="mcgee-schmidt-1985" /><Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />. Julier and Uhlmann summarize 35 years of experience: the EKF is difficult to implement and tune, and reliable only for systems almost linear on the time scale of the updates <Cite id="julier-uhlmann-2004" />. Li and Mourikis proved that standard EKF visual-inertial odometry is inconsistent because of how its Jacobians are computed, so it underestimates its uncertainty <Cite id="li-mourikis-2013" />. Smith, Self, and Cheeseman's stochastic map propagated first-order covariance estimates of spatial relationships and required small angular errors, because it linearizes inherently nonlinear relationships <Cite id="smith-1990" />.

edits.before: The failure mode is baked into that construction. Linearization is valid near the estimate, and the estimate is exactly what you are unsure about. When the nonlinearity is strong over the region the covariance covers, the propagated $\Sigma$ stops describing the true error: the filter grows overconfident, the covariance and the actual error part ways, and the estimate can diverge. Reasoning about the covariance structure of spatial estimates is where the robotics community learned these lessons, in the work of Smith, Self, and Cheeseman on uncertain spatial relationships <Cite id="smith-1990" />. The standard escapes are to keep the Gaussian but drop the analytic linearization, pushing a few deterministically chosen sample points through the true nonlinearity instead, which is the unscented Kalman filter of Julier and Uhlmann <Cite id="julier-uhlmann-1997" />, or to drop the Gaussian assumption entirely and carry the belief as a set of particles <Cite id="thrun-2005" />.
edits.after: The unscented Kalman filter of Julier and Uhlmann keeps the Gaussian and pushes deterministically chosen sample points through the true nonlinearity <Cite id="julier-uhlmann-1997" />. Particle filters drop the Gaussian assumption and carry the belief as a set of particles <Cite id="thrun-2005" />. Invariant filters on Lie groups remove the dependence on the estimate: in the contact-aided invariant EKF, neither the linearized error dynamics nor the linearized observation model depends on the current state estimate <Cite id="hartley-inekf-2019" />. The equivariant filter EqVIO is a consistent visual-inertial estimator with lower linearization error <Cite id="eqvio-2022" />. GTSAM 4.3.0, released September 18, 2026, ships EKF and invariant-EKF infrastructure, equivariant filtering and EqVIO support <Cite id="gtsam-4-3-2026" />.

Kschischang, Frey, and Loeliger's 2001 paper unified inference on such graphs under the sum-product algorithm <Cite id="kschischang-2001" />. With Gaussian factors, the most probable trajectory solves one sparse nonlinear least-squares problem <Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />:

edits.before: Dellaert and Kaess's 2006 Square Root SAM formulation jointly estimates the <Term id="slam">SLAM</Term> trajectory and landmark map. With known data associations, Gaussian process and measurement models, a uniform landmark prior, and the initial reference frame fixed, this gives a nonlinear least-squares problem. Nonlinear optimization solves successive linearized systems: for a full-rank system, QR acts on the measurement Jacobian, while Cholesky acts on the information matrix. Variable ordering controls fill-in and therefore the cost <Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />. iSAM made the approach incremental, updating only the part of the factorization a new measurement actually touches <Cite id="kaess-2008" />. With Gaussian noise models, iSAM2 uses a Bayes tree for incremental nonlinear least-squares estimation, with incremental variable reordering and relinearization. An update re-eliminates the affected cliques and their ancestors, then reattaches unaffected subtrees. Changes in estimates can still propagate down the tree; relinearization and partial-update thresholds trade accuracy for computation. The update cost is not constant: large loop closures can be as expensive as a batch solution <Cite id="kaess-2012" />. This family is what modern visual-inertial odometry and offline mapping run on: GTSAM, a BSD-licensed C++ library that implements smoothing and mapping using factor graphs and Bayes networks, powers many such systems in academia and industry <Cite id="gtsam-2026" />; Forster and colleagues' on-manifold preintegration is what made high-rate inertial data fit the framework, collapsing anywhere from a small number to hundreds of IMU readings between two keyframes into a single preintegrated factor <Cite id="forster-2017" />.
edits.after:
Dellaert and Kaess's 2006 Square Root SAM jointly estimates the <Term id="slam">SLAM</Term> trajectory and landmark map, assuming known data associations, Gaussian models, a uniform landmark prior and a fixed initial frame. It solves successive linearized systems, by QR on the measurement Jacobian or Cholesky on the information matrix, and variable ordering sets fill-in and cost <Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />. The iSAM method updates only the part of the factorization a new measurement touches <Cite id="kaess-2008" />. iSAM2 adds a Bayes tree with incremental reordering and relinearization: an update re-eliminates the affected cliques and their ancestors, then reattaches unaffected subtrees. Thresholds trade accuracy for computation, and a large loop closure can cost as much as a batch solve <Cite id="kaess-2012" />.

GTSAM is a BSD-licensed C++ library that implements sensor fusion for robotics and computer vision using factor graphs <Cite id="gtsam-2026" />. Version 4.3 moved to C++17 and added experimental CUDA nonlinear optimization and several legged-state-estimation implementations <Cite id="gtsam-4-3-2026" />. Building on Lupton and Sukkarieh's preintegration, Forster and colleagues' on-manifold version collapses anywhere from a few to hundreds of IMU readings between two keyframes into one factor <Cite id="forster-2017" />.

edits.before: Cadena and colleagues describe a classical SLAM period from 1986 to 2004 that included EKF, Rao-Blackwellised particle-filter and maximum-likelihood approaches, followed by an algorithmic-analysis period from 2004 to 2015. Their survey presents MAP estimation, often expressed using factor graphs, as the de-facto standard formulation, but also highlights EKF-based systems with state-of-the-art performance. It reports a smaller filtering-versus-MAP performance gap when EKF linearization is accurate, sliding-window filters are used, and inconsistency is addressed. Graphs do not remove resource limits: the survey discusses unbounded graph growth and information-loss tradeoffs in sparsification, not a universal rule that smoothing wins <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. What a robot then keeps from that estimate, a point cloud, a signed-distance field, a mesh, and which of those a planner can actually consume, has its own treatment in [scene representation and mapping](/classical/scene-representation).
edits.after: Cadena and colleagues describe a classical SLAM period from 1986 to 2004, with EKF, Rao-Blackwellised particle-filter and maximum-likelihood approaches, and an algorithmic-analysis period from 2004 to 2015 <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. In Rao-Blackwellized grid mapping, each particle carries its own map <Cite id="grisetti-gmapping-2007" />. The survey treats MAP estimation, often over factor graphs, as the de facto standard but notes EKF systems with state-of-the-art performance. The gap shrinks when EKF linearization is accurate, sliding windows are used and inconsistency is addressed, and graphs still face unbounded growth and information loss under sparsification <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. The MSCKF sliding-window filter keeps 3D feature positions out of the state and is optimal up to linearization errors <Cite id="msckf-2007" />. OKVIS argues that nonlinear optimization offers superior accuracy while staying tractable through sparsity <Cite id="okvis-2014" />. [Scene representation and mapping](/classical/scene-representation) covers what a robot keeps from the estimate.

edits.before: State estimation is the layer of the classical stack that learning has penetrated least, and the reason is the honest number: a covariance you can trust is worth more than a point estimate that is usually right. Learned components mostly enter as better sensors. A learned depth model or a learned visual-odometry frontend feeds the same filter or factor graph, which keeps the uncertainty bookkeeping classical even when the measurement model is a network.
edits.after: Learned components mostly enter classical estimators as measurements with uncertainty. Backprop KF optimizes a filter as a deterministic computation graph, so convolutional networks can read raw images <Cite id="backprop-kf-2016" />. TLIO regresses 3D displacement and its uncertainty from IMU data and fuses both into a stochastic cloning EKF <Cite id="tlio-2020" />. AirIO pairs a learned inertial model with an uncertainty-aware EKF for aggressive UAV flight <Cite id="airio-2025" />. MAC-VO learns a metrics-aware keypoint covariance and uses it to weight pose graph optimization <Cite id="mac-vo-2024" />.

edits.before: One connection is deeper than the rest. The latent-dynamics world models in the [world-models](/world-models/latent-dynamics) module are learned state estimators in disguise: a recurrent latent state that predicts the next observation is a belief state by another name, trained end to end instead of derived. What learning changes is where the models come from; the predict-update structure underneath has survived every regime change since 1960.
edits.after: Tartan IMU, pretrained on over 100 hours of multi-platform data, reports a 36% ATE improvement over specialized models and learns online at 200 FPS <Cite id="tartan-imu-2025" />. GAIT estimates legged-robot state without an explicit contact estimator and outperforms contact-aided model-based methods on a Unitree Go1 <Cite id="gait-2026" />. MASt3R-SLAM builds on a learned two-view reconstruction prior and keeps loop closure and second-order global optimization <Cite id="mast3r-slam-2024" />.

edits.before: With estimation in place, the classical stack closes: [kinematics](/classical/kinematics) describes the body, [planning](/classical/motion-planning) picks the motion, [control](/classical/control) executes it, and estimation tells all three what actually happened.
edits.after: [Latent-dynamics world models](/world-models/latent-dynamics) act as learned belief states. PlaNet's latent dynamics model has deterministic and stochastic transition components trained with variational inference <Cite id="planet-2018" />. DreamerV3 learns a model of the environment and improves its behaviour by imagining future scenarios <Cite id="dreamerv3-nature-2025" />.

edits.before: Many apparent estimator failures begin before the filter. A camera exposure, encoder reading and inertial sample that carry the same receipt time may describe different physical instants. Feeding them into a precise model creates a confident estimate of a state that never existed. Clock offset, transport delay and rolling-shutter timing belong in the measurement contract beside frame and covariance.
edits.after: Fusing visual and inertial measurements requires each measurement's precise sampling time <Cite id="li-mourikis-temporal-2014" />. Samples with the same receipt time can describe different instants, and most consumer cameras use rolling shutters that capture each pixel row at a slightly different time <Cite id="li-rolling-shutter-2013" />. The camera-IMU offset can be a state variable, locally identifiable except in a few degenerate motions <Cite id="li-mourikis-temporal-2014" />. OpenVINS calibrates the camera-to-IMU time offset in its sliding-window filter <Cite id="openvins-2020" />, and Kalibr estimates time offsets to a fraction of the smallest measurement period <Cite id="kalibr-2013" />.

edits.before: Test the pipeline in that order: verify clock domains and timestamp monotonicity, measure sensor latency, validate transforms, then tune process and measurement noise. Replay a recorded motion and inspect innovations by sensor; persistent directional residuals suggest calibration or timing bias instead of random noise. The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) covers spatial and temporal residuals, while the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) covers timestamped message and transform interfaces. A larger covariance can express uncertainty. It cannot repair misassociated time.
edits.after: Persistent directional residuals in per-sensor innovations point to calibration or timing bias instead of random noise. GrandTour, which its authors call the largest open-access legged-robotics dataset, supplies RTK-GNSS and total-station ground truth <Cite id="grandtour-2026" />. The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) covers temporal residuals, and the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) covers timestamped interfaces.

edits.before: In June 2026, Dantong Niu, Yuke Zhu, Trevor Darrell and colleagues described T-Rex, which pairs a 100-hour tactile-rich dataset with a vision-language-action model that reads high-frequency touch through a variable-rate mixture-of-transformers and a temporal tactile encoder. On 12 tasks requiring delicate force control and deformable-object manipulation, its average success rate was more than 30% higher than the strongest baseline's <Cite id="t-rex-2026" />.
edits.after:
In June 2026, Dantong Niu, Yuke Zhu, Trevor Darrell and colleagues described T-Rex, which pairs a 100-hour tactile-rich dataset with a vision-language-action model that reads high-frequency touch through a variable-rate mixture-of-transformers and a temporal tactile encoder. On 12 tasks requiring delicate force control and deformable-object manipulation, its average success rate was more than 30% higher than the strongest baseline's <Cite id="t-rex-2026" />.

In September 2026, Enyi Wang and Yan Wang of Tsinghua University's Institute for AI Industry Research and colleagues reported TacDyn-WAM, a world action model that predicts learned tactile representations instead of reconstructing tactile images. On five real-robot tasks with 60 demonstrations each, it averaged 71.0% success, 16 points above the tactile policy FTP-1, and 85.0% after pretraining on about 6,000 real visuo-tactile trajectories <Cite id="tacdyn-wam-2026" />.

Behavior cloning fails in closed loop for a precise reason: a policy with per-step error ε on the expert's state distribution can accumulate cost that grows quadratically with episode length, because each mistake carries the robot into states the expert never visited . Over a T-step episode the worst-case cost scales as $$ \underset{\text{behavior cloning}}{O(\varepsilon T^2)} \qquad \underset{\text{DAgger}}{O(\varepsilon T)} $$ where the second bound is what DAgger buys by repeatedly relabeling the states the policy actually visits . Action chunking attacks the same bound from a different side: it shrinks the effective horizon. Instead of predicting one action per inference, the policy predicts a sequence of k actions at once, so the number of sequential decisions in an episode drops by a factor of k. Try “One move at a time” and then “100 moves per plan”. That curve is ACT's own ablation: 1% success one action at a time, 44% at a hundred. Everything else in this module explains why those two numbers are so far apart. ## ACT: chunking with a CVAE Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT), introduced together with the ALOHA bimanual teleoperation hardware, wraps chunking in a conditional variational autoencoder . During training, an encoder reads the demonstration's action sequence and produces a latent style variable. At test time the policy decodes a chunk conditioned on camera images, joint positions, and the latent clamped to zero.
The 14 action coordinates are six arm joints and one gripper coordinate per arm. The ACT hardware description names two six-DoF ViperX arms; the paper's “7+7=14 DoF” shorthand counts the gripper coordinates too, so it never means seven arm joints . Mobile ALOHA explicitly describes its 14 arm-action coordinates as including two continuous gripper actions . The objective in the card follows ACT's implementation description, which specifies L1 reconstruction; the printed algorithm uses MSE, with a weighted KL regularizer in both accounts . The paper is internally inconsistent here; the card pins the L1 choice for this implementation and claims nothing about a universal ACT objective. ### The chunk-size dial Chunk size is a real bias/variance dial. The curve above comes from the paper's two simulated MuJoCo tasks (Cube Transfer and Bimanual Insertion), averaged over four settings (each task trained on scripted and on human demonstrations, temporal ensembling disabled): ACT measures 1% success at k=1, 44% at k=100, and a decline at k=200 and k=400 as the policy becomes effectively open-loop . Too small and compounding error returns; too large and the policy stops reacting to the world mid-chunk. Chunking does not reduce the per-decision error ε. It reduces the number of decisions, T divided by k, over which that error compounds. The bias you pay is commitment: the world can change inside a chunk, and the policy will not notice until the next inference. ## Temporal ensembling and its limits The pinned ACT reference implementation uses temporal ensembling: it queries the policy at every timestep and averages the retained predictions for the current action in oldest-to-newest order . Its weights are $w_i = \exp(-m \cdot i)$, where $i = 0$ is the earliest retained prediction and $m = 0.01$. Thus the oldest retained prediction has the largest weight; increasing $m$ reduces the relative weight of newer predictions. The example below starts with already-selected predictions and illustrates the weighted average; the reference code's nonzero-buffer selection rule stays outside it. ```python title="temporal_ensembling.py" # ACT reference convention: preds contains current-step predictions already # selected and ordered oldest-to-newest. Index 0 is the oldest retained # prediction, not "zero chunks ago". Reference m=0.01. This helper does not # reproduce ACT's raw-buffer nonzero occupancy filter. def temporal_ensemble(preds: list[np.ndarray], m: float = 0.01) -> np.ndarray: weights = np.exp(-m * np.arange(len(preds))) # w_i = exp(-m * i) weights /= weights.sum() return np.tensordot(weights, np.stack(preds), axes=1) ``` For an illustrative scalar example **after selection**, oldest-to-newest predictions `[0, 10, 20]` at $m = 0.01$ receive normalized weights approximately `[0.33667217, 0.33332222, 0.33000561]` and yield `9.93333444`. This does not exercise the reference occupancy filter, which would discard a literal zero scalar in the raw buffer. The RTC experiment used π0.5 with five denoising steps: model latency was 76 ms for the baselines and 97 ms for RTC, plus 10 to 20 ms over LAN. The tested temporal-ensembling variants triggered protective stops at **an additional 100 or 200 ms** of injected delay, measured on top of the existing model and network latency . The accompanying blog reports averages over six tasks, ten episodes per task; this is an experimental result and carries no universal failure threshold . When two overlapping chunks commit to different modes, say left versus right around an obstacle, the weighted average can be an action that belongs to neither mode. The robot drifts between strategies instead of committing to one.
Demonstrations contain pauses that are unpredictable from a Markovian single-step state. Both ACT and [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy) document robots freezing when the policy cannot represent the pause . Temporal context is the fix; the backbone's size is beside the point.
Real-Time Chunking (RTC) reframes the hand-off between chunks as an inpainting problem on the flow or diffusion trajectory: actions that will already have executed are frozen, the overlapping middle is partially attended to, and the remainder is generated fresh . In the reported π0.5 experiment, RTC showed no degradation in average task throughput through +200 ms of injected delay, without retraining . This evaluates RTC on a flow-matching policy; it does not establish adoption by later generations of [the pi line](/manipulation/pi-line). edits.before:
An action space is the interface between a policy and the rest of the robot. It decides what the network predicts, which errors the low-level controller must absorb, how frequently inference must run, and whether data from two embodiments can share labels. Calling both outputs “actions” hides differences large enough to reverse a model comparison.

The useful question is not which action space is best. It is which responsibilities should live in the learner and which should remain in a controller with explicit geometry, dynamics and safety limits.

Try the check below and choose the Cartesian interface only if the controller underneath can uphold its side of the contract.
edits.after: An action space is the interface between a policy and the rest of the robot: what the network predicts, which errors the controller absorbs, how often inference runs and whether embodiments share labels. In Open X-Embodiment, the same seven numbers can mean absolute or relative positions or velocities <Cite id="open-x-embodiment-2023" />. Try the check below.

edits.before:
An action is more than a vector. A complete action contract specifies:

1. **Coordinates:** joint, Cartesian, object-relative or another frame.
2. **Semantics:** absolute target, delta, velocity, force, torque or controller parameter.
3. **Timing:** control rate, prediction horizon and how stale predictions are handled.
4. **Execution:** interpolation, clipping, inverse kinematics, feedback control and safety limits.

Two papers can both report a seven-dimensional action while meaning different things. One may emit a relative end-effector delta integrated by a task-space controller; another may emit absolute joint targets under a separate low-level loop. The output widths match; the learning problems do not.
edits.after: A contract names coordinates (joint, Cartesian, object-relative or another frame), semantics (absolute target, delta, velocity, force, torque or controller parameter), timing (rate, horizon and stale-prediction handling) and execution (interpolation, clipping, inverse kinematics, feedback and safety limits). DROID records equivalent commands in several action spaces <Cite id="droid-2024" />, and robosuite's controllers span joint and Cartesian spaces <Cite id="robosuite-2020" />.

edits.before: **Joint position targets** are one imitation-learning baseline. On matched leader-follower setups, demonstrated joint angles can serve as labels after checking calibration and gripper conventions. ACT uses absolute joint-and-gripper targets for its two ViperX arms, predicted in chunks <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />.
edits.after: Joint position targets are a common imitation baseline: on matched leader-follower rigs, demonstrated angles become labels after calibration checks. ACT uses the leader arms' joint positions as actions, predicting chunks of absolute joint-and-gripper targets for two ViperX arms <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. The controller interpolates, enforces limits and closes a fast loop, but one shoulder angle moves different arms differently.

edits.before:
The advantage is repeatability on one mechanism. The controller can interpolate targets, enforce joint limits and close a high-rate loop below the policy. The cost is embodiment specificity. A shoulder angle on one arm does not describe the same end-effector motion on another.

**Joint velocity targets** encode increments instead of absolute configurations. Integrating them requires current joint state and can drift; equal velocities can produce different Cartesian motion on different robots.

Both representations require an accurate kinematic model. The [kinematics module](/classical/kinematics) derives the forward map and Jacobian that connect joint motion to the hand <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />.
edits.after: Joint velocity targets encode increments and can drift when integrated. The [kinematics module](/classical/kinematics/) derives the forward map and Jacobian that both need <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />. In locomotion RL, target joint angles with local feedback beat raw torques for learning speed, robustness and motion quality <Cite id="peng-action-space-2016" />.

edits.before: Cartesian actions describe what the tool should do: translate, rotate, open or close. Relative deltas encode motion from the current pose instead of an absolute target; their range and frame still need to be specified. They also provide a plausible shared label for arms whose joint counts and link lengths differ.
edits.after: Cartesian actions say what the tool should do: translate, rotate, open or close. Relative deltas from the current pose can label arms with different joint counts and link lengths alike once range and frame are fixed. Each robot then needs inverse kinematics or an operational-space controller, singularity handling and joint-limit avoidance. Khatib's 1987 IEEE Journal on Robotics and Automation paper on the operational space formulation unifies motion and force control <Cite id="khatib-1987" />.

edits.before: The simplicity is above the waterline. Underneath, each robot needs inverse kinematics or an operational-space controller, singularity handling, joint-limit avoidance and a named reference frame. Khatib's 1987 IEEE Journal of Robotics and Automation paper, "A Unified Approach for Motion and Force Control of Robot Manipulators: The Operational Space Formulation," frames motion and force control as one problem and gives the operational-space formulation its name <Cite id="khatib-1987" />.
edits.after: Euler angles and quaternions are discontinuous as network outputs, while 6D representations are continuous <Cite id="rotation-continuity-2018" />. Axis-angle increments must also name the tool or world frame.

edits.before:
Rotation needs special care. Euler-angle deltas have discontinuities and depend on axis order. Axis-angle and exponential coordinates are compact but must define whether the increment is expressed in the tool or world frame. A six-number action is not portable until that convention is written down.

NVIDIA says GR00T N1.7 adopts relative end-effector deltas shared across robot and human embodiments <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />. That is a representation choice with consequences beyond preprocessing: it determines which non-robot data can become a useful target.
edits.after: NVIDIA says GR00T N1.7 shares relative end-effector deltas across robot and human embodiments, so priors learned from human video transfer directly to robot control <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />. Its N1.6 notes find relative actions smoother and more accurate than absolute ones but prone to error accumulation on small datasets <Cite id="gr00t-n1-6-2025" />. UMI pairs relative-trajectory actions with latency matching to deploy one policy on several arms <Cite id="umi-2024" />, and a unified end-effector-relative representation was critical for cross-embodiment transfer in matched VLA pretraining ablations <Cite id="vla-scaling-alignment-2026" />. X-VLA instead adds a separate set of learnable soft-prompt embeddings for each data source, which act as embodiment-specific prompts <Cite id="x-vla-2025" />.

edits.before: **Torque actions** expose low-level dynamics and contact directly; position and impedance controllers can express related behaviors through their own feedback loops. They also demand a high control rate, accurate timing, actuator-specific scaling and a safety layer that remains effective when the learned output is wrong. Franka's control interface documentation states that libfranka can send real-time control values at 1 kHz using five different control modes, including gravity- and friction-compensated joint-level torque commands <Cite id="franka-fci-docs" />.
edits.after: Torque actions expose dynamics and contact; Levine et al. mapped raw images to motor torques <Cite id="levine-visuomotor-2015" />. They need a high rate, accurate timing, actuator-specific scaling and a safety layer that holds when the output is wrong. libfranka sends 1 kHz commands in five modes, including gravity- and friction-compensated joint torque <Cite id="franka-fci-docs" />. Rudin et al.'s locomotion pipeline sends joint-position targets to a PD controller instead <Cite id="rudin-2021" />.

edits.before: **Impedance actions** are a useful middle layer. The policy selects a pose target plus stiffness and damping, while a controller converts the error into forces. Variable end-effector impedance has been studied explicitly as an RL action space for contact-rich tasks <Cite id="martin-martin-2019" />. It gives learning control over compliance without asking it to synthesize every torque sample.
edits.after: Impedance actions sit between: the policy picks a pose target plus stiffness and damping, and a controller turns error into force. Hogan judged position or force control alone inadequate for manipulation <Cite id="hogan-1985" />. Variable end-effector impedance has been studied as an RL action space for contact-rich tasks <Cite id="martin-martin-2019" />. Task-space impedance references needed the fewest samples in a comparison with torque, joint PD and inverse dynamics <Cite id="varin-action-spaces-2019" />, and Adaptive Compliance Policy's predicted compliance beats position-only visuomotor policies by over 50% <Cite id="acp-2024" />.

edits.before: One design keeps compliance targets in the learned policy while a separately tested controller owns the fast feedback.
edits.after: FACTR 2 (Carnegie Mellon and Waseda University, June 2026) estimates external joint torque from motor current, with no force sensor. Across five long-horizon tasks, its force-aware policy beat prior force-aware policies by over 17% in task progress <Cite id="factr-2-2026" />. T-Rex feeds high-frequency touch to a VLA through a variable-rate mixture of transformers and beat its strongest baseline by over 30% average success on 12 tasks <Cite id="t-rex-2026" />.

edits.before:
An <Term id="action-chunking">action chunk</Term> predicts several future steps per inference. In ACT's ablations, chunking improved ACT and the two baselines the authors retrofitted with it, and the CVAE objective proved essential on human demonstrations: removing it cut success on the two simulated human-data tasks from 35.3% to 2% <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. Diffusion Policy also predicts a horizon and executes only the first portion before replanning <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />.

Chunks can represent temporally coordinated motion, but their inference cost depends on how often the policy replans. Longer open-loop execution can leave a stale plan when the scene changes. If contact makes the world diverge after the first few steps, the remaining chunk reflects an observation that is no longer current. Receding-horizon execution, temporal ensembling and real-time chunk replacement <Cite id="real-time-chunking-2025" /> are different answers to that problem.

Report the chunk horizon and the executed horizon separately. A predicted chunk length alone does not tell the reader whether all actions run open loop or when the policy replans.

Diffusion Policy executes the first part of a predicted horizon, then replans <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />. edits.before:
<Term id="behavior-cloning">Behavior cloning</Term> is the oldest way to make a robot imitate a person: record what an expert did, treat each observation as an input and the expert's action as the label, and fit a policy $\pi(a \mid s)$ by supervised learning. The idea predates deep learning. ALVINN (1988) used a three-layer back-propagation network with camera and laser-range inputs. It was trained on simulated road images and tested on NAVLAB, a modified Chevy van; training on real images while a human drives was proposed future work, and the reported training procedure uses simulated road images <Cite id="alvinn-1988" />.

The appeal is obvious: no reward function to design, no exploration to manage, just regression onto demonstrations. The failure mode is equally specific, and nearly every architectural innovation in learned manipulation since 2023 is a partial answer to it. Supervised learning assumes that test inputs come from the same distribution as training inputs. A robot running in closed loop violates that assumption with its own actions.
edits.after: <Term id="behavior-cloning">Behavior cloning</Term> is imitation learning cast as supervised learning: a policy $\pi(a \mid s)$ is regressed onto [expert actions](/how-robots-work/#puppeteer) given expert observations. In closed loop the robot's own actions choose its future inputs, breaking the i.i.d. assumption, so <Term id="compounding-error">errors compound</Term> <Cite id="ross-bagnell-2010" />.

edits.before: This deterministic toy illustrates persistent drift; it is neither a source benchmark nor a task-cost theorem. Each prediction adds an error that grows with the drift. Try “A teacher corrects it” to watch DAgger-style relabeling cut the summed deviation.
edits.after: Try “A teacher corrects it” to watch DAgger-style relabeling <Cite id="dagger-2011" /> cut the summed deviation.
