edits.after: ## Learned and orchestrated hierarchies, 2025 to 2026

edits.before: Read the current frontier systems side by side and the same pattern appears in each one.
edits.after: Figure's Helix pairs a 7B VLM at 7 to 9 Hz with an 80M-parameter visuomotor policy at 200 Hz, trained end-to-end <Cite id="helix-2025" />. GR00T N1 runs its VLM at 10 Hz on an L40 GPU and its action module at 120 Hz <Cite id="gr00t-n1-2025" />, and Fast-in-Slow partially shares parameters between the two, reaching 117.7 Hz with eight-action chunks <Cite id="fast-in-slow-2025" />.

edits.before:
- **π0.5** co-trains on robot data, semantic subtask labels, and multimodal web tasks. Pretraining uses discrete tokens; post-training adds the continuous action expert. At inference, the same model predicts a high-level language subtask and then conditions low-level actions on it. High-level inference runs less frequently than low-level action inference; this does not establish a numerical inference rate <Cite id="pi05-2025" />.
- **Hi Robot** uses two separately trained policies initialized from PaliGemma: a high-level VLM and a low-level π0 VLA. The high level reads camera images and open-ended instructions, then sends simpler language commands to the low level, which also receives images and robot state. High-level inference is rerun when one second has elapsed or new human feedback arrives; users can intervene with text or transcribed speech and can signal a return to the prior task <Cite id="hi-robot-2025" />. The training combines human-labelled demonstrations with synthetic interactions, with a separate high-level policy for each task domain in the reported experiments. Evaluations cover table bussing, sandwich making and grocery shopping. This hierarchy does not guarantee successful execution: the authors report missing high-level memory, low-level instruction violations and difficulty recovering from dropped objects <Cite id="hi-robot-2025" />.
- **Gemini Robotics 1.5** combines both patterns: with thinking enabled, the VLA appends natural-language reasoning to its context before emitting actions; the agentic system pairs it with a separate GR-ER 1.5 orchestrator. ER's thinking-token budget is varied in the report's embodied-reasoning evaluations, with task-dependent benefits. Internal VLA thinking and the external orchestrator therefore coexist <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />.
- **GO-2** is described by AgiBot as a unified system with an asynchronous two-module hierarchy. Its Semantic Planning Module (System 2) generates action intents through Progressive Refinement at a lower frequency; its Action Following Module (System 1) combines intents and real-time observations through Residual Refinement at a higher frequency. The announcement does not give numerical rates or establish that the modules share one set of weights. Teacher forcing is a training mechanism and adds no third runtime layer <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />.
- **Helix 02** extends Figure’s S2/S1 architecture with a learned S0 controller. Figure describes S2 semantic behavior sequencing, S1 full-body joint targets at 200 Hz from vision, touch, and proprioception, and a 10M-parameter S0 network that outputs joint-level actuator commands at 1 kHz. These are vendor-reported rates for different stages and do not compare as inference-throughput results; the announcement does not specify S2’s numerical rate <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />.
- **π0.7** can condition its actions on visual subgoal images. At runtime a BAGEL-initialized world model produces these images from observations and the subtask instruction. Subtask and image generation run in separate threads, while VLA inference uses the latest available outputs <Cite id="pi07-2026" />. **π0.6-MEM** uses a high-level policy to predict the next language subtask and an updated language-memory summary from previous memory, observations, and the task. Its low-level policy conditions actions on the subtask and a shorter observation history. This is MEM’s memory mechanism and makes no claim about shared runtime implementation with π0.7 or a disclosed update frequency <Cite id="mem-2026" />.
edits.after: π0.5 co-trains on robot data, semantic subtask labels and multimodal web tasks, pretraining with discrete tokens and adding a continuous action expert in post-training. At inference the same model predicts a language subtask and then actions conditioned on it, running the high level less often; its mobile manipulator takes 50 Hz targets in 50-action chunks. Training also predicts relevant bounding boxes before subtask labels and adds box-annotated indoor and household data to the web mixture <Cite id="pi05-2025" />.

edits.before: The π0.5 paper reports 50 Hz target commands for its mobile-manipulator setup and predicts 50 actions per chunk, but that does not establish one chunk inference per second. The interactive keeps 1 chunk/s only as a schematic cadence. Figure reports Helix 02 S1 joint targets at 200 Hz and S0 actuator commands at 1 kHz. GO-2’s lower/higher module frequencies and the other schematic intervals are not numerical rate measurements. The extra GO-2 motor-tick lane is a drawing device; no third module is disclosed <Cite id="pi05-2025" /> <Cite id="helix-02-2026" /> <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />.
edits.after: Hi Robot trains two policies from PaliGemma: a high-level VLM that turns images and open-ended instructions into simpler language commands, and a low-level π0 VLA that also reads robot state. The high level reruns after one second or on new human feedback, and users can intervene by text or speech or return to the prior task. Training mixes human-labelled demonstrations with synthetic interactions, with one high-level policy per domain, across table bussing, sandwich making and grocery shopping. The authors report missing high-level memory, low-level instruction violations and trouble recovering dropped objects <Cite id="hi-robot-2025" />.

edits.before: ## The verdict
edits.after: π0.7 can condition actions on subgoal images from a BAGEL-initialized world model; subtask and image generation run in separate threads, and the VLA uses the latest outputs <Cite id="pi07-2026" />. In π0.6-MEM, a high-level policy predicts the next language subtask and an updated memory summary, and the low-level policy acts on the subtask and a shorter observation history <Cite id="mem-2026" />. VISTA's high-level world-model planner raises the same VLA from 14% to 69% in novel scenarios <Cite id="vista-2026" />. SeeQ, from Saksham Singh, Aviral Kumar and colleagues at Carnegie Mellon (September 2026), puts the subtask inside the value function: it names the active subtask in language before estimating that subtask's value <Cite id="seeq-2026" />.

edits.before: Two claims are worth stating plainly, and both need framing.
edits.after: AgiBot describes GO-2 as a unified system with an asynchronous two-module hierarchy: a lower-frequency System 2 generates action intents through Progressive Refinement, and a higher-frequency System 1 combines them with observations through Residual Refinement. It gives no numerical rates or shared-weights claim; GO-2 trains with teacher forcing <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />. Figure's Helix 02 adds S0 beneath S2's behavior sequencing and S1's 200 Hz full-body joint targets from vision, touch and proprioception. S0 is a 10M-parameter network that outputs actuator commands at 1 kHz; Helix 02 does not restate the S2 rate <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />.

edits.before: First: **the five cited examples place high-level guidance at different interfaces.** π0.5 uses the same model to infer a language subtask and actions conditioned on it <Cite id="pi05-2025" />. The π0.6-MEM report describes a high-level policy that predicts the next subtask and updated language memory, with a low-level policy conditioned on that subtask and recent observations <Cite id="mem-2026" />. π0.7 can use subgoal images from a BAGEL-initialized world model; when those images are used, subtask and image generation run asynchronously in separate threads <Cite id="pi07-2026" />. With thinking enabled, Gemini Robotics 1.5 appends natural-language reasoning to the VLA context before actions, while its agentic system retains a separate GR-ER 1.5 orchestrator <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />. AgiBot describes GO-2 as a lower-frequency semantic planning module paired with a higher-frequency action-following module <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />. This is a comparison of reported mechanisms; it supplies no evidence that separate planners have been superseded across the field.
edits.after: With thinking on, Gemini Robotics 1.5 appends natural-language reasoning before acting, and its agentic system adds a separate GR-ER 1.5 orchestrator whose useful thinking budget depends on the task. ER 1.5 also produces point sequences that trace trajectories <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />. Google made ER 1.5 broadly available as a high-level model that can call a VLA or user-defined functions <Cite id="gemini-robotics-er-15-dev-2025" />. In [Gemini Robotics 2](/manipulation/generalist-policies/), DeepMind calls ER 2 the robot's high-level brain; it coordinates with the VLA and tracks multi-minute tasks <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />. Google says ER 2 hands off motor execution to any lower-level VLA and reports 57.4% accuracy on progress classification <Cite id="gemini-robotics-er-2-2026" />.

edits.before: Second: **geometric supervision in training does not establish the disappearance of geometric reasoning at runtime.** π0.5’s paper describes training the model to predict relevant bounding boxes before subtask labels, and adding indoor-scene and household-object data with bounding-box annotations to its web-data mixture <Cite id="pi05-2025" />. Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5 also reports complex pointing, including point sequences that can represent motion trajectories and paths <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />. That is evidence of a geometric reasoning capability; it proves nothing about a specific deployed controller using a keypoint loop. The scope here is those reported mechanisms, short of an exhaustive inventory of 2026 frontier systems; no field-wide absence of runtime keypoint interfaces is claimed.

In a controlled 2026 study on a real ALOHA, the best hierarchy placed 12 of 15 fruits, against 9 for a naive hierarchy and 3 for a flat VLA. In-network hierarchy can fail too: in a waypoint pipeline adapted from π0.5, erasing waypoint endpoints barely changed success. edits.before:
<Term id="knowledge-insulation">Knowledge insulation</Term> is a training recipe that keeps action learning from damaging a vision-language-action model's pretrained backbone. RT-2 represents robot actions as tokens, using the discretization introduced for RT-1: each continuous action dimension is divided into 256 uniform bins. Its robot inputs pair a camera image with a task instruction <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. π0 instead adds a continuous <Term id="flow-matching">flow-matching</Term> action expert to a pretrained <Term id="vision-language-model">VLM</Term> <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. Knowledge Insulation, studied by Physical Intelligence in 2025, combines the two: discrete actions train the backbone’s representations while a continuous-action expert trains alongside it without sending gradients back into the backbone.

<Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> The paper distinguishes the earlier two-stage π0.5 recipe from simultaneous single-stage training.

<Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" /> The research note calls this single-stage model π0.5 + KI.

The barrier is below, on the backward pass. Turn off "Protect language skills", which removes the stop-gradient: the damage the recipe exists to prevent runs straight back into the pretrained backbone.
edits.after: <Term id="knowledge-insulation">Knowledge insulation</Term> (KI) is a training recipe that keeps action learning from damaging a vision-language-action model's pretrained backbone. Discrete FAST action tokens train the backbone, while a stop-gradient keeps a <Term id="flow-matching">flow-matching</Term> action expert's gradients out of it <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />. Turn off "Protect language skills" to remove the stop-gradient.

edits.before: The 7.5x figure compares training steps to similar table-bussing performance; inference latency and equal wall-clock training budgets are different axes. The paper reports about 20% extra training cost from the combined objectives. The paper's architecture details describe a 2B language-model backbone within the complete VLM and a 300M action expert; the research note labels the complete VLM as 3B <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.
edits.after: ## Origins

edits.before: ## What naive joint training breaks
edits.after: RT-2 tokenizes each continuous action dimension into 256 uniform bins, as RT-1 did <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. Physical Intelligence's 2025 KI note judges such fixed-bin tokens unsuitable for high-frequency, precise or fluent motions <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />, and the 7B token-based OpenVLA decodes at about 6 Hz on an RTX 4090 <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. π0 adds a continuous action expert to a pretrained <Term id="vision-language-model">VLM</Term> <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. π0.5 trained 280k steps on discrete tokens, then post-trained a randomly initialized flow-matching expert <Cite id="pi05-2025" />. KI makes this a single stage <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />, called π0.5 + KI <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.

edits.before: The paper studies a pretrained VLM with a newly initialized continuous-action expert. It finds that expert gradients can interfere with the image encoder and language backbone during adaptation, slowing learning and weakening language following. The proposed explanation is interference with pretrained representations; the paper measures no claim that every early gradient is large or that the model can never recover <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
edits.after: ## Naive joint training

edits.before: One qualitative example illustrates the problem with π0: instructed to bus a spoon into the bin, it grasps trash instead. The research note describes the target as the dish container and explicitly calls its explanation a hypothesis: disrupted language processing may lead the model to learn other correlations first <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />. The note’s phrase "not suitable for high-frequency, precise, or fluent motions" refers to the earlier simple fixed-bin action representation and to no other tokenized-action method <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.
edits.after: Fine-tuning a pretrained network through a random head distorts its features and raises out-of-distribution error <Cite id="kumar-finetuning-distorts-2022" />. The KI paper finds the same in VLAs: gradients from a new action expert degrade the backbone, slowing training and weakening language following. Told to bus a spoon into the bin, π0 grasps trash <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />. The note hypothesizes that disrupted language processing lets the model learn other correlations first <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.

edits.before: ## The recipe, in three parts
edits.after: ChatVLA calls this spurious forgetting, robot training overwriting visual-text alignments <Cite id="chatvla-2025" />, and InstructVLA reports catastrophic forgetting of vision-language skills in existing VLAs <Cite id="instructvla-2025" />. Between robot tasks, pretrained VLAs resist forgetting; simple experience replay sometimes removes it <Cite id="vla-continual-forgetting-2026" />.

edits.before: Knowledge Insulation separates the learning signals <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />:
edits.after: ## Recipe

edits.before:
1. **The action expert trains with flow matching** to generate continuous action chunks at inference.
2. **The backbone learns from discrete FAST <Term id="action-tokenization">action tokens</Term>**, alongside general vision-language and robot-planning data. FAST normalizes actions, applies a DCT separately along time for each action dimension, scales and rounds the coefficients, then uses byte-pair encoding to compress the flattened sequence. Coefficient quantization is lossy; BPE losslessly compresses the resulting integer sequence <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />.
3. **Stop-gradient blocks the expert’s updates to the backbone.** The expert can attend to the image/language/state prefix and its own continuous-action tokens. It does not attend to FAST action tokens, and the backbone does not attend to the expert. The attention equations apply stop-gradient to the backbone keys and values read by the expert, leaving forward information available while blocking that backward path <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
edits.after:
1. The action expert trains with flow matching, regressing vector fields of fixed conditional probability paths <Cite id="lipman-flow-matching-2022" />, and generates continuous action chunks at inference <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
2. The backbone learns from discrete FAST <Term id="action-tokenization">action tokens</Term> plus vision-language and robot-planning data. FAST normalizes actions, applies a DCT to each action dimension over time, and scales and rounds the coefficients, the lossy step. Byte-pair encoding then compresses the flattened sequence losslessly <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />.
3. Stop-gradient blocks the expert's updates to the backbone. The expert attends to the image, language and state prefix and to itself, never to FAST tokens; the backbone never attends to it. Stop-gradient on the backbone keys and values the expert reads keeps the forward path and cuts the backward one <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

edits.before: The figure at the top of this module walks both passes through the two stacks, including the failure mode with the barrier removed.
edits.after: Training both outputs costs about 20% more compute. The paper's backbone is a 2B language model with a 300M expert <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />; the note labels the complete VLM 3B <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />, the size of PaliGemma, which pairs a SigLIP-So400m encoder with Gemma-2B <Cite id="paligemma-2024" />.

edits.before: ## Why the barrier alone is not enough
edits.after: FAST tokens are π0.5 + KI's training representation and continuous flow actions its runtime output <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />, so a [comparison matrix](/manipulation/comparison-matrix/) needs both columns.

edits.before: Stopping expert gradients is not the same as adapting the backbone for robot control. Without another robot-learning signal, the pretrained backbone’s representations remain unadapted to the task. In the paper’s frozen-backbone ablation, shirt-folding performance is reported as 0%; that is an outcome for this tested configuration and proves nothing about all frozen-backbone policies <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
edits.after: ## Limits and alternatives

edits.before: FAST-token supervision supplies the missing action-learning signal while the gradient barrier blocks updates from the newly initialized expert. The paper also finds that vision-language co-training can give the joint-training baseline good language following even without stop-gradient. The evidence supports the combined recipe; it makes no claim that continuous gradients always destroy knowledge or that cross-entropy guarantees perfect preservation <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
edits.after: Stopping expert gradients does not adapt the backbone: with the backbone frozen, the paper's shirt-folding policy scores 0%. FAST supervision supplies that signal, and vision-language co-training can give plain joint training good language following without stop-gradient <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

edits.before: ## What it buys
edits.after: GR00T N1 freezes the language part of its VLM <Cite id="gr00t-n1-2025" />. NVIDIA reports that N1.5, which froze the whole VLM among other changes, raised real GR-1 language following from 46.6% to 93.3% <Cite id="gr00t-n1-5-2025" />; N1.6 unfreezes the top 4 layers <Cite id="gr00t-n1-6-2025" />. BLIP-2 bridges frozen image encoders and language models <Cite id="blip2-2023" />. VLM2VLA writes actions as language and trains only LoRA adapters <Cite id="vlm2vla-2025" />. UAM keeps over 95% of its VLM's multimodal capability with no freezing, gradient stopping or co-training <Cite id="uam-forgetting-2026" />.

edits.before: The paper separates two table-bussing comparisons. For a generalist trained on many embodiments, π0 needs 7.5 times as many training steps as π0.5 + KI to reach similar performance. For specialist models trained on one embodiment, the authors report that π0-FAST needs twice the wall-clock time to solve the task. That second result is task-completion time; a generic twofold inference-latency multiplier or a comparison across all robot tasks is a different claim <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.
edits.after: Figure's Helix instead backpropagates from its fast policy into the VLM through their shared latent vector <Cite id="helix-2025" />. HybridVLA trains discrete and diffusion action prediction together, using a collaborative recipe against interference <Cite id="hybridvla-2025" />.

edits.before: The table-bussing task starts with 12 objects and scores correct placement into the dish and trash receptacles. The paper reports ten episodes per real-world task and policy. In a separate mobile-manipulation object-generalization experiment, the robot moves unseen objects from a counter into an already-open drawer; the research note says web-data co-training boosted generalization most in that comparison. These are different evaluation populations and form no single combined benchmark <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.
edits.after: ## Results

edits.before: Language following also improves in the items-in-drawer comparison, but remains imperfect. The paper notes that VLM co-training can help the joint-training baseline follow language even without stop-gradient <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
edits.after: A many-embodiment π0 generalist needs 7.5 times the training steps of π0.5 + KI to reach similar table-bussing performance. Single-embodiment π0-FAST specialists need twice the wall-clock time from slow inference <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />. Table bussing starts with 12 objects for dish and trash receptacles, at ten episodes per task and policy. When a mobile robot moves unseen objects into an open drawer, web-data co-training boosts generalization most, and language following improves but stays imperfect <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.

edits.before: ## Both, in different places
edits.after: In third-party fine-tuning, π0.5 with KI stays near zero on out-of-distribution task perturbations; KI alone does not fix out-of-distribution language generalization <Cite id="apt-action-expert-pretraining-2026" />. A reimplemented co-training plus KI baseline trailed standard behavior cloning on mean LIBERO-PRO and LIBERO-Plus success <Cite id="anchor-align-2026" />, though the dual FAST and flow objective mitigates forgetting more than flow alone <Cite id="garg-self-demonstrated-control-2026" />. Across seven VLAs, VQA co-training goes with better knowledge retention <Cite id="act2answer-2026" />. In Toyota Research Institute's 89-policy co-training study, training only on robot data cost the VLM backbone its ability to generate language, and co-training with effective modalities restored it <Cite id="lbm-cotraining-2026" />.

edits.before: In the π0.5 + KI recipe, action representation has two roles: FAST tokens provide training supervision for the backbone, while the flow-matching expert generates continuous actions at inference. The expert’s gradients do not update the backbone <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />. A [comparison matrix](/manipulation/comparison-matrix) should distinguish training representation from runtime output and resist forcing this model into a single binary category.

edits.before: ## Related later models
edits.after: openpi's public π0.5 checkpoints were trained with KI, but the repository serves only the flow-matching head <Cite id="openpi-repo-2024" />. Outside groups therefore reimplemented the FAST loss and stop-gradient <Cite id="garg-self-demonstrated-control-2026" />. LAP-3B blocks expert gradients and runs at 25 Hz on an RTX 4090 <Cite id="lap-2026" />, and LabVLA applies KI to a FAST-pretrained Qwen3-VL-4B <Cite id="labvla-2026" />. Dexmal and StepFun's 2B DM0 (February 2026) adopts a hybrid gradient strategy "inspired by Knowledge Insulation": on embodied data, action-expert gradients stay out of the VLM <Cite id="dm0-2026" />. A 2026 review sorts implementations into gradient stopping, as in π0.5-KI and π0.6, and inpainting <Cite id="stulp-full-stack-transfer-2026" />.

edits.before: π0 grafts a second transformer onto a pretrained <Term id="vision-language-model">vision-language model</Term> <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. The first set of weights handles image and text tokens and is initialized from PaliGemma. The second set, the action expert, handles robotics-specific tokens and has approximately 300M parameters in the paper’s implementation. The structural point matters for anyone implementing one: the action expert is a second set of transformer weights inside a single model, in the paper's words "a single transformer with two sets of weights (also known as experts)." It is a full transformer whose 50 action tokens attend into the backbone's activations at every layer through shared self-attention, with a bidirectional mask among themselves. Observations are 2 or 3 RGB images, tokenized language, and proprioceptive state; the model predicts H = 50 actions. The paper’s UR5e and Franka setups run at 20 Hz and execute 16 actions before another inference; other tested robots run at 50 Hz and execute 25 <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. edits.before: FAST normalizes each action dimension, applies a discrete cosine transform along time, scales and rounds the coefficients, and byte-pair-encodes their flattened sequence. The control period at 50 Hz is 20 ms, and every component in the loop, cameras, network, preprocessing, model, spends from that budget. The earlier modules treated action chunking as an algorithmic choice; this module is about what happens when the algorithm meets the clock. Real-time execution turns out to be a first-class architectural problem. The way a policy hands off from one chunk to the next while inference is still running changes what the robot physically does, and the naive ways to do it fail in documented, measurable ways . The teaching model below compares one synchronous inference with a 20 ms tick. Its slider uses illustrative scaling and a deliberately chosen 3.0B reference coordinate; it is not a hardware profiler or a proof that a chunked 50 Hz robot controller cannot run. Slide the model-size control and the missed-deadline count follows the new inference time.
## Where the milliseconds go The Real-Time Chunking paper reports a π0.5 latency breakdown with inference on an RTX 4090 in bfloat16, five denoising steps and a wired LAN. Across 50 inference calls during a real episode, mobile total latency is 138.98 ± 6.71 ms: model 96.89 ± 0.16, network 21.20 ± 3.12, image resizing 11.22 ± 5.00 and other work 9.67 ± 3.20 ms. The non-mobile total is 108.76 ± 2.34 ms; the ± values are one standard deviation. Image resizing uses an Intel i7-1260P NUC in the mobile case and an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X workstation in the non-mobile case . At 50 Hz, the mean totals span about 6.95 and 5.44 control periods. Their reciprocals, about 7.20 and 9.19 inferences per second, do not establish the actual replanning or robot-control rate; the RTC experiment uses chunked execution. Jiang, Clemons, Sankaralingam and Kozyrakis study the scaling picture with VLA-Perf, a roofline-based analytical model with no hardware-wide profiling campaign behind it . Its predictions assume optimistic software and attainable peak compute and memory bandwidth. The paper compares them with an optimized π0 Triton implementation on an RTX 4090: the implementation reaches 73.3 to 82.6% of predicted throughput under the tested one-, two- and three-camera settings, with 10 flow-matching steps, chunk size 63 and an empty language prompt. In its separate B100 π0 model sweep, increasing denoising steps from 10 to 50 at chunk size 50 multiplies action-expert latency by 5, but total VLA latency by 2.15. Increasing chunk size from 50 to 250 at 10 steps raises expert latency by 40% and total latency by 11% . Chunk size matters less in this experiment, though it still carries cost; expert latency is one part of the pipeline. ## The hardware wall VLA-Perf predicts π0 inference at 162.5 Hz on H100 and 19.0 Hz (52.57 ms) on Jetson Thor, excluding network latency . The baseline is 2.7B parameters: a 0.4B vision encoder, 2B VLM and 0.3B action expert. It models three 224×224 cameras, 32 language tokens (800 input tokens total), 14 action dimensions, chunk size 50, 10 denoising steps and batch size one, using BF16 or FP16 where BF16 is unsupported. These are inferences per second; robot and controller Hz are different quantities, and sensing and robot execution latency sit outside the analysis. The 9.1B π0-L result, 3.9 Hz on Thor, is for a hypothetical variant built from a 1.1B SigLIP-Giant encoder, 6.5B Llama2 backbone and 1.5B action expert; no measured deployed policy sits behind it . The control-loop interactive above uses a separate teaching curve; its 3.0B coordinate is not the paper’s 2.7B baseline. VLA-Perf defines 10 Hz inference as “acceptable” and 100 Hz as “high-performance” relative to common camera rates; these are the authors’ analysis targets and bind no universal robot-control requirement . For their on-device π0 setup, the predicted 19 Hz exceeds the first target. They propose smaller models, fewer denoising steps or lower-precision quantization to approach 100 Hz. This does not show that future hardware cannot help. The baseline π0 vision encoder, VLM and action expert are all memory-bound on the modeled Thor configuration. On the other evaluated GPUs, vision and VLM work are compute-bound while the action expert remains memory-bound. The component-scaling experiment finds approximately linear latency growth with parameter count . These results do not characterize every possible workload on Thor. The study assumes adequate model accuracy and evaluates BF16/FP16 inference; its quantization recommendation is not an FP4/FP8 2 to 4× speedup result or an accuracy-loss validation. Server placement also depends on the modeled network . For synchronous π0 inference, RTX 4090 over WiFi 6 is 38.7 ms versus Thor’s 52.6 ms, but RTX 4090 over 5G is slower at 55.7 ms. B100 over the same 5G model is 27.8 ms. The paper's network model assumes WiFi 6 upload/download bandwidth of 560/800 Mbps and 3.5 ms base latency, versus 80/500 Mbps and 10 ms for 5G. In the cloud examples, B100 with Ethernet 10G plus the fast-cloud link is 23.4 ms, while 4G plus the slow-cloud link is 273.4 ms. The fast/slow cloud links use 10/1 Gbps and 10/100 ms base latency; the 4G hop uses 19/75 Mbps and 25 ms. These are specified link assumptions and measure no arbitrary deployed network. ## Three ways to hand off a chunk Suppose inference takes d milliseconds. The policy has emitted a chunk, the robot is executing it, and a new chunk is on the way. What happens at the boundary is a design decision, and there are three options on the table. **Synchronous execution** waits: execute a chosen part of the current chunk, pause while the next one is computed, then resume. Do not equate that executed part with the whole predicted chunk: π0 predicts 50 but executes 16 actions on the 20 Hz UR5e/Franka setups or 25 on the other 50 Hz robots . The RTC paper evaluates stopping between chunks as a π0.5 baseline. Its discussion links altered motion dynamics to distribution shift, and its real-world comparison reports faster progress with RTC even after inference pauses are removed from elapsed time . **Naive switching** never waits: the instant the new chunk arrives, execution jumps to it. There is no dead time, but there is a discontinuity. The new chunk was inferred from an observation d milliseconds old, the world has moved since, and the two chunks disagree about what to do right now. The command steps by the full disagreement in a single control tick: a jerk event the hardware feels. **Temporal ensembling**, ACT’s 2023 method, queries the policy at every timestep and combines predictions for that same timestep with weights $w_i=\exp(-mi)$. The paper assigns $i=0$ to the oldest retained prediction, so for positive $m$ older predictions receive greater weight; it does not say newer observations dominate . Averaging predictions from different action modes need not produce a valid action. In the RTC paper’s π0.5 real-robot comparison, both temporal-ensembling variants trigger the robot’s protective stop at +100 and +200 ms of injected latency . **Real-Time Chunking** guides generation of a new action chunk while the current one executes. Its inpainting guidance assigns weight 1 to the first $d$ actions, which will execute during inference; weight 0 to the non-overlapping tail; and decaying intermediate weights to the remaining overlap. These are soft-mask guidance weights; the paper makes no claim that transformer attention itself is partially disabled . The original method is an inference-time procedure for diffusion/flow policies without retraining. In the paper’s six-task π0.5 real-robot evaluation with five denoising steps, RTC’s aggregate throughput shows no degradation over the tested +0, +100 and +200 ms injected delays. The paper also illustrates precise match-lighting at total inference delay above 300 ms; that is not a claim that every dynamic task succeeds under every such delay . The comparison below is an illustrative hand-off model; it implements and measures nothing of RTC. One delay slider drives three constructed velocity traces. The values use arbitrary velocity units; the 0.30 per-tick threshold is a discontinuity proxy standing in for physical jerk. Its five-tick linear blend is a teaching assumption and models neither transformer attention nor the paper’s inpainting solver. ## Training the tolerance in π0.7 uses a training-time version of Real-Time Chunking. Its paper states that training simulates delays of 0 to 12 timesteps, corresponding to a maximum inference latency of 240 ms on a 50 Hz robot . Treat that as a stated training setting; it carries no measured worst-case latency guarantee and proves no production deployment. The experiments predict 50 actions and execute either 15 or 25; UR5e robots run at 20 Hz and the other tested robots at 50 Hz. The paper does not assign the execution choices to specific robots . In September 2026, Fanding Huang, Cheng Chi, Zhi Wang and colleagues reported ChunkTrust, which infers how many actions to execute before replanning from the policy's own outputs while it runs. Its training-free horizon selector combines the stability of each generated chunk with its continuity with the actions already executed. Over all 50 RoboTwin2.0 tasks it raised π0.5's task-averaged success by 6.80 percentage points, and on four real household tasks it raised the mean normalized process score from 50.4% to 57.5% . ## Spending the step budget VLA-Perf’s π0 sweep shows that step count affects expert and total latency by different factors . The following papers report their own step settings. pi0 integrated its flow with 10 Euler steps per chunk . pi0.6 cut that to 5, landing at 63 ms per chunk on a single H100 with three cameras . pi0.7 stays at 5 . These three source-specific choices do not establish field-wide nonadoption of one-step distillation or show that it matters chiefly on edge hardware. π0.7’s paper documents its own five-step policy with training-time RTC and surveys no other laboratories . VLA-Perf’s values are analytical roofline predictions; no five-GPU robot measurement stands behind them. Its π0-L is hypothetical, and it assumes adequate accuracy and validates no quantization accuracy. The control-loop curve is a separate teaching model: it places the 52.57 ms reference at a deliberately chosen 3.0B coordinate instead of the paper’s 2.7B, uses linear and power-law scaling, and reports reciprocal inference rate, a different quantity from robot rate. The hand-off traces use arbitrary velocity units and an illustrative 0.30 per-tick discontinuity proxy; the five-tick blend is not RTC’s inpainting algorithm. The retained measured references have different meanings: RTC reports 108.76 ms non-mobile and 138.98 ms mobile mean total latency in its RTX 4090/wired-LAN setup; the π0.6 model card reports 63 ms per chunk on one H100 with five steps and three cameras. π0.7’s 240 ms is its stated maximum simulated training delay at 50 Hz and carries no measured tolerance guarantee. None of these is a shared controller-frequency benchmark.

edits.before: RL fine-tuning is the use of reinforcement learning to improve a pretrained robot policy from its own successes and failures. <Term id="imitation-learning">Imitation learning</Term> gets a policy that is good on the demonstration distribution and brittle off it, because small per-step errors compound into states the demonstrator never visited <Cite id="dagger-2011" />. Physical Intelligence states the operational version of the same problem: it is relatively easy to get a VLA to succeed at a task some of the time, and quite hard to make it succeed reliably <Cite id="pistar06-blog-2025" />. Reinforcement learning is the only mechanism in the toolbox that learns from failure as well as from success. The obstacle is cost: naive online RL on a multi-billion-parameter VLA, on real hardware, at control rates, is infeasible. Everything in this module is a way around that constraint, and by 2026 the field has converged on a small set of recipes that demonstrably work.
edits.after: RL fine-tuning is the use of reinforcement learning to improve a pretrained robot policy from its own successes and failures. <Term id="imitation-learning">Imitation learning</Term> is brittle off the demonstration distribution because errors compound <Cite id="dagger-2011" />, and Physical Intelligence finds reliable success much harder than occasional success <Cite id="pistar06-blog-2025" />.

edits.before: Modern policies emit actions through diffusion or <Term id="flow-matching">flow-matching</Term> heads, and that choice breaks the standard policy-gradient machinery. <Term id="ppo">PPO</Term>-style updates need the log-likelihood of the action the policy actually took; for a flow-matching head the "action" is the endpoint of an ODE integration, and its likelihood under the model is intractable. For two years this was the standard argument for why RL could not touch the frontier VLAs directly. Three methods dissolve it in different ways <Cite id="dppo-2024" /> <Cite id="conrft-2025" /> <Cite id="pi-rl-2026" />.
edits.after: <Term id="ppo">PPO</Term> runs several epochs of minibatch updates on a clipped surrogate objective <Cite id="ppo-2017" />, which needs the likelihood of each action taken. <Term id="flow-matching">Flow matching</Term> trains by regressing vector fields along fixed conditional probability paths <Cite id="lipman-flow-matching-2022" />, so the executed action's log-likelihood is intractable <Cite id="pi-rl-2026" />. Applying online RL directly to large VLAs also brings training instability and compute beyond most local machines <Cite id="ire-vla-2025" />.

edits.before: **DPPO** (Ren et al., 2024) embeds the diffusion denoising process inside the environment MDP. Each policy action in this combined MDP is a denoising transition with an analytically evaluable Gaussian likelihood; the environment advances and supplies reward only after the final denoising step. PPO updates the denoising policy while the environment dynamics stay fixed. Environment-discounted advantages are multiplied by a separate denoising discount that downweights earlier, noisier steps. The value function depends on the environment state. The paper also fine-tunes only the last selected denoising steps, using a frozen original network for earlier steps and a trainable copy for the selected steps <Cite id="dppo-2024" />.
edits.after: DPPO (Ren et al., 2024) follows DDPO, which posed diffusion denoising as a multi-step decision problem <Cite id="ddpo-2023" />. DPPO embeds denoising inside the environment MDP: each denoising transition has an analytic Gaussian likelihood, and the environment advances and pays reward only after the final step. Environment-discounted advantages are multiplied by a denoising discount that downweights earlier, noisier steps, and the value function depends on the environment state. Only the last selected denoising steps are fine-tuned, with a frozen copy of the network for earlier ones <Cite id="dppo-2024" />.

edits.before: Perry Dong, Kuo-Han Hung, Tian Gao, Dorsa Sadigh and Chelsea Finn (Stanford) attack the problem from the value side. Their EXPO algorithm trains a large flow or diffusion base policy with a stable imitation objective, plus a lightweight Gaussian edit policy that nudges sampled actions toward higher value; an on-the-fly policy then executes and backs up the value-maximizing candidate among the base and edited actions, sidestepping gradient propagation through the denoising chain. The paper reports up to 2-3x sample-efficiency improvements on average over prior methods, both when fine-tuning a pretrained policy from offline data and when training online from it <Cite id="expo-2025" />.
edits.after: EXPO (Perry Dong, Qiyang Li, Dorsa Sadigh and Chelsea Finn; ICLR 2026) trains a large flow or diffusion base policy with a stable imitation objective plus a lightweight Gaussian edit policy that nudges sampled actions toward higher value. EXPO reports up to 2 to 3× better sample efficiency on average, both when fine-tuning a pretrained policy from offline data and when using offline data to train online <Cite id="expo-2025" />.

edits.before: Dong and Finn's September 2026 position, stated in a joint blog post, is that the field is at its GPT-2 moment: capable demos from pretrained VLAs, and no shared post-training recipe behind them. In their words, “RL shows incredible promise in training frontier robotics models, but it is not yet a recipe. It's a craft.” They argue robotics needs what language modeling has: a stable algorithm plus standard protocols for reward specification, resets, human input, hyperparameters and initialization. They attach their own limits to EXPO-FT: a human still defines success, resets the scene and intervenes; longer horizons strain the value function; and “Nineteen minutes of robot interaction is not nineteen minutes of post-training,” because gradient updates on a model this size dominate wall-clock time <Cite id="perry-dong-post-training-2026" />.

The inspected PLD and DSRL sources do not establish a code or weight release. Recap's inspected report, blog and model card do not establish model-specific checkpoint availability or licensing; this is not a claim that the model is closed. The openness notes keep those source scopes with each row <Cite id="dppo-2024" /> <Cite id="conrft-2025" /> <Cite id="hil-serl-2024" /> <Cite id="pi-rl-2026" /> <Cite id="pistar06-2025" /> <Cite id="pistar06-blog-2025" /> <Cite id="pi06-model-card-2025" /> <Cite id="pld-2026" /> <Cite id="expo-ft-2026" /> <Cite id="dsrl-2025" />.
edits.after: RL-100, published in Science Robotics in July 2026, applies one clipped-PPO objective within the denoising process across offline and online stages. It reports 1000 of 1000 successful episodes on eight real tasks, including 250 consecutive successes on one <Cite id="rl-100-2025" />. LWD runs offline-to-online RL on a fleet of 16 dual-arm robots, where one generalist policy reaches 95% average success across eight real tasks <Cite id="lwd-2026" />. SOP's performance scales near-linearly with the number of robots in its fleet <Cite id="sop-2026" />. ENPIRE gives coding agents the whole real-robot improvement loop, from scene reset and verification to training-code changes. Its authors report 99% success on dexterous tasks such as fastening a zip tie, and eight agents cut the time to near-perfect pin insertion from over 1.5 hours to about 40 minutes <Cite id="enpire-2026" />.

edits.before: Liu et al.'s NeurIPS 2025 study reports that PPO beat the tested DPO/TPO and GRPO implementations in its OpenVLA pick-and-place setup, where preferences and returns came from sparse task rewards. The authors summarize the main OOD comparison with supervised fine-tuning as stronger semantic and execution generalization, with comparable visual robustness; arbitrary new-task generalization sits outside the test. The January 2026 revision adds a preliminary sim-to-real trial and an articulated-object task to a narrower main-text limitation statement. Its results are mixed: SFT wins on the articulated-task visual average and rephrased instructions, and on the action-chunking multi-receptacle test <Cite id="rl-vla-generalization-2025" />.
edits.after: Liu et al.'s NeurIPS 2025 study finds PPO beats the tested DPO/TPO and GRPO implementations for OpenVLA pick-and-place with sparse task rewards. Against supervised fine-tuning it reports stronger semantic and execution generalization and comparable visual robustness. A September 2025 revision adds appendix tests: a preliminary sim-to-real trial, an action-chunking comparison and an articulated-object task. SFT wins the articulated task's visual average and rephrased instructions, and the action-chunking multi-receptacle test. The main-text limitations still say all experiments are simulated pick-and-place <Cite id="rl-vla-generalization-2025" />.

edits.before: Peng et al.'s PAIR-VLA study addresses a related limitation in how RL treats visual changes. In simulated ManiSkill3 pick-and-place experiments with OpenVLA and π0.5, it adds paired-view invariance and sensitivity objectives to PPO: preserve action distributions for task-preserving changes and separate them for target-pose changes. The authors argue that task rewards alone give limited guidance about this distinction and report improved OOD success over standard PPO under the tested visual shifts. The sensitivity-only ablation loses to PPO on target-pose success; the separate camera-view experiment, using a different task-preserving view construction, also trails PPO slightly in-distribution despite its OOD gains. That comparison leaves reward design unisolated as the cause of a pre-to-post-RL loss of robustness; its task-preserving views also rely on simulator object masks, and real-world transfer remains untested <Cite id="pair-vla-2026" />.
edits.after: PAIR-VLA adds paired-view invariance and sensitivity objectives to PPO in simulated ManiSkill3 pick-and-place with OpenVLA and π0.5. It preserves action distributions under task-preserving changes and separates them under target-pose changes, arguing that task rewards alone give limited guidance here, and reports better OOD success than PPO under the tested shifts. The sensitivity-only ablation loses to PPO on target-pose success, the camera-view variant trails PPO slightly in-distribution, the task-preserving views rely on simulator object masks, and real-world transfer is untested <Cite id="pair-vla-2026" />.

<Callout variant="warn" title="How to read these numbers">

Reward specification is unsolved: nearly every method uses a hand-written success detector or a VLM-based one, which is itself a reward-hacking surface. Recap's results are vendor-reported; the inspected report, blog and model card do not establish model-specific weight-release or license terms. Treat the table above as a map of mechanisms; rankings across these protocols would mislead.

edits.before:
The robot learning curriculum for ML engineers is a staged path through the robotics that policy experiments depend on, from coordinates to evaluation. Machine learning gives you optimization, representation learning, sequence models and experimental discipline. It does not give you coordinate frames, control loops, contact dynamics or a reliable definition of task success. A useful robot-learning roadmap therefore starts at the interfaces where a model meets a machine. The aim is not to learn all of robotics before training a policy. It is to learn each dependency just before an experiment needs it.

The shortest route has six layers: geometry, data, imitation, action representation, evaluation and deployment. Foundation models and reinforcement learning sit on top of those layers; they do not remove them.

Try the check below and choose the baseline you would run before a larger policy. The option names the first experiment that separates a data problem from a model problem.
edits.after: The robot learning curriculum for ML engineers is a staged path through the robotics that policy experiments depend on: geometry, data, imitation, action representation, evaluation and deployment, each learned just before an experiment needs it. A 2025 open tutorial runs from behavior cloning and reinforcement learning to generalist policies <Cite id="robot-learning-tutorial-2025" />. Try the check below.

edits.before: ## Stage 1: make coordinates concrete
edits.after: ## Stage 1: coordinates

edits.before: Start with [kinematics](/classical/kinematics); the reason is that observations and actions live in frames, with no expectation that every learner implements an inverse-kinematics solver. You should be able to answer four questions without looking at the training code: which frame an object pose uses, which frame an end-effector delta uses, whether rotations compose on the left or right, and where joint limits enter. *Modern Robotics* supplies the compact mathematical vocabulary for this layer <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />.
edits.after: Start with [kinematics](/classical/kinematics/): know which frame an object pose and an end-effector delta use, whether rotations compose on the left or right, and where joint limits enter. *Modern Robotics* supplies the vocabulary <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />, and Tedrake warns that sloppy kinematic notation "will inevitably lead to confusion and bugs" <Cite id="tedrake-manipulation-2026" />.

edits.before: Then read [calibration](/classical/calibration) and [state estimation](/classical/state-estimation). A policy can appear stochastic when the real defect is a drifting camera transform or a timestamp mismatch. This is the first habit to import from robotics: before changing the network, prove that the target the network sees refers to the same physical state as the action in the label.
edits.after: Then study [calibration](/classical/calibration/) and [state estimation](/classical/state-estimation/): a drifting camera transform or timestamp mismatch can look like a stochastic policy. Kalibr estimates sensor time offsets to a fraction of the smallest measurement period <Cite id="kalibr-2013" />.

edits.before: ## Stage 2: treat data collection as a system
edits.after: ## Stage 2: data as a system

edits.before: Robot data is a coupled record; a folder of images carries none of the coupling. Each transition needs synchronized observations, the commanded action, the action actually realized when available, robot state, task identity, termination, and enough provenance to reproduce the split. DROID reports 76k episodes collected across 13 institutions <Cite id="droid-2024" />.
edits.after: Each transition couples synchronized observations, commanded and realized actions, robot state, task identity, termination and provenance; RLDS stores such episodes losslessly <Cite id="rlds-2021" />. Among public [datasets](/data-hardware/datasets/), Open X-Embodiment pools 22 robots from 21 institutions <Cite id="open-x-embodiment-2023" />, and DROID holds 76k trajectories from 13 institutions <Cite id="droid-2024" />.

edits.before: Before collecting at scale, record ten episodes and replay them end to end. Plot timestamp gaps. Render actions back onto the robot state. Verify units and rotation conventions. Check that train and test environments do not share nearly identical episodes. These checks are cheaper than discovering after substantial teleoperation that camera and joint streams were misaligned.
edits.after: Before scaling, record ten episodes and replay them: plot timestamp gaps, render actions onto the robot state, and check units and rotation conventions. Past a threshold per environment or object, more demonstrations add little, and diversity matters far more <Cite id="lin-data-scaling-laws-2024" />.

edits.before: The [datasets guide](/data-hardware/datasets) explains the public corpora; the [robot-learning stack](/data-hardware/robot-learning-stack) explains the machinery around your own.
edits.after: GELLO collects demonstrations more reliably than VR controllers or 3D spacemice <Cite id="gello-2023" />, and LeRobot spans the [robot-learning stack](/data-hardware/robot-learning-stack/) from motor middleware to dataset streaming <Cite id="lerobot-paper-2026" />.

edits.before: ## Stage 3: establish the imitation baseline
edits.after: ## Stage 3: imitation baseline

edits.before: Behavior cloning is supervised learning with a closed-loop distribution shift. The learner sees expert states during training and its own imperfect states at deployment. DAgger formalized why errors compound and why collecting corrective actions on learner-induced states changes the problem <Cite id="dagger-2011" />.
edits.after: [Behavior cloning](/manipulation/bc-foundations/) trains on expert states and then visits its own, a closed-loop distribution shift. DAgger formalized why errors compound and why corrective labels on learner-induced states change the problem <Cite id="dagger-2011" />. HG-DAgger adapts it for human experts, whose labels can degrade without full control <Cite id="hg-dagger-2019" />.

edits.before: Run the smallest baseline that can close the loop. For image observations, that might be an encoder plus an MLP or a short transformer. Keep one camera, one task and one action convention. If it fails, inspect data alignment, normalization, reset diversity and label multimodality before adding scale.
edits.after: Run the smallest closed-loop baseline, such as an image encoder and MLP, on one camera, task and action convention. If it fails, inspect alignment, normalization, reset diversity and label multimodality before adding scale. robomimic found results sensitive to design choices, demonstration quality and stopping criteria <Cite id="robomimic-2021" />.

edits.before: Once the baseline is legible, add temporal structure. ACT predicts action chunks and temporally ensembles overlapping predictions at execution <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. Diffusion Policy represents a multimodal distribution over action sequences and executes it in a receding horizon <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />. Both methods produce temporal action sequences; their objectives and inference procedures differ, so compare their controller and execution contracts directly.
edits.after: Add temporal structure. ACT predicts action chunks and temporally ensembles overlapping predictions <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. Diffusion Policy models a multimodal distribution over action sequences, executed in a receding horizon <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />.

edits.before: ## Stage 4: choose the action contract
edits.after: ## Stage 4: action contract

edits.before: Read [action spaces](/manipulation/action-spaces) before comparing policy architectures. Joint positions are mechanism-specific. End-effector deltas can provide a shared task-space convention when each robot has a compatible controller and frame convention. Torque and tokens impose different low-level and decoding costs.
edits.after: Among [action spaces](/manipulation/action-spaces/), joint positions are mechanism-specific; end-effector deltas share a task-space convention across compatible controllers and frames. Torque and tokens add low-level and decoding costs, and per-dimension binning tokenizers handle high-frequency dexterous data poorly <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />.

edits.before: The action representation is part of the dataset. Changing it changes the labels, the controller under the policy, the error modes and often the set of robots that can share data. No model comparison is clean if those changed at the same time.
edits.after: The action representation is part of the dataset: it fixes the labels, the controller, the error modes and which robots can share data. Change it apart from the model. Variable-impedance end-effector actions improved sample efficiency and safety in three manipulation tasks <Cite id="martin-martin-2019" />.

edits.before: ## Stage 5: add pretraining only after the interfaces hold
edits.after: ## Stage 5: pretraining

edits.before: A VLA is useful when task language, semantic generalization or multi-task transfer matters. OpenVLA made the recipe reproducible: fuse spatial and semantic vision features into a language backbone, then fine-tune it to emit robot actions <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. The starting checkpoint is valuable, but the same data alignment and action-space constraints remain.
edits.after: A VLA helps when language, semantic generalization or multi-task transfer matters. OpenVLA made the recipe reproducible: fuse spatial and semantic vision features into a language backbone, then fine-tune it to emit actions <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. π0 pretrains on over 10,000 hours of robot data <Cite id="pi0-2024" />, and SmolVLA trains on one GPU yet performs comparably to VLAs ten times larger <Cite id="smolvla-2025" />.

edits.before: Ask what pretraining is supposed to provide. If the missing capability is recognizing an unseen object category, web-scale vision-language pretraining is a plausible intervention. If the failure is a gripper colliding because the hand-eye transform is wrong, it is not. The [foundation-model guide](/manipulation/foundation-models) separates transfer claims from architecture labels.
edits.after: [Pretraining](/manipulation/foundation-models/) can help recognize an unseen object category; a wrong hand-eye transform still needs calibration. In TRI's blind, randomized trials, multitask pretraining made policies more successful and robust and taught new tasks with a fraction of the data <Cite id="tri-lbm-2025" />.

edits.before: ## Stage 6: make evaluation harder than the demo
edits.after: ## Stage 6: evaluation

edits.before: Create the evaluation protocol before the main training run. Define task success, failure, intervention, reset and timeout. Separate familiar configurations from changed objects, backgrounds, lighting and geometry. Report trial counts and uncertainty alongside the average. LIBERO-Plus tests VLA robustness under controlled changes to object layout, camera viewpoint, robot initial state, language, lighting, background texture and sensor noise <Cite id="libero-plus-2025" />.
edits.after: Define success, failure, intervention, reset and timeout before the main run, and separate familiar configurations from changed objects, backgrounds, lighting and geometry. Papers often give little or no information on run counts, initial conditions, success criteria or statistics <Cite id="kress-gazit-evaluation-2024" />. Report trial counts and uncertainty; STEP's sequential test needs up to 32% fewer trials than prior tests <Cite id="optimal-stopping-2025" />.

edits.before: Open-loop loss is a diagnostic; the result sits elsewhere. A useful evaluation pyramid has four levels:
edits.after: Open-loop loss is a diagnostic. Check datasets for leakage, action distributions, timestamps and annotations; open-loop error and calibration on held-out episodes; closed-loop success, interventions and failures under controlled shifts; and deployment cycle time, recovery, resets, faults and operator load. LIBERO-Plus shifts object layout, camera viewpoint, initial state, language, lighting, background and sensor noise <Cite id="libero-plus-2025" />. SIMPLER's simulated scores correlate with real performance <Cite id="simpler-2024" />, and RoboArena's double-blind pairwise trials rank generalist policies better than centralized evaluation <Cite id="roboarena-2025" />. For deployment, [ROS 2](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers/) was rebuilt with the production-grade features ROS 1 lacked <Cite id="ros2-science-robotics-2022" />.

edits.before:
1. **Dataset checks:** leakage, action distributions, timestamps and annotation quality.
2. **Open-loop checks:** prediction error and calibration on held-out episodes.
3. **Closed-loop checks:** success, interventions and failure modes under controlled shifts.
4. **Deployment checks:** cycle time, recovery, resets, hardware faults and operator load.
edits.after: ## Simulation and RL

edits.before: ## When simulation and RL enter
edits.after: Simulation tests controller stability, robustness to parameter variation and safe reward optimization. Domain randomization aims to make the real world look like one more simulated variation <Cite id="tobin-2017" />. Isaac Lab targets large-scale, multi-modal robot learning <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />; measure its dynamics gap to the hardware.

edits.before:
Simulation belongs where it answers a concrete question: whether a controller is stable, whether a policy survives parameter variation, or whether a reward can be optimized safely. Isaac Lab is designed for large-scale, multi-modal robot-learning workflows and is an appropriate environment once the task's contact and sensor assumptions are credible <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />. It is not a substitute for measuring the gap between its dynamics and the hardware.

Offline RL belongs when a logged dataset contains meaningful variation in outcome quality and a reward can rank that variation. Online RL belongs when the system can explore safely, reset automatically and evaluate cheaply. When reward, safe exploration and resets are missing, <Term id="imitation-learning">imitation learning</Term> is a practical first use of collected demonstrations.
edits.after: Offline RL learns from logged data without new collection <Cite id="offline-rl-tutorial-2020" />, so it fits logs whose outcome quality varies and a reward can rank. Online RL needs safe exploration, automatic resets and cheap evaluation; SERL bundles an off-policy learner with reward computation, resets and a controller <Cite id="serl-2024" />. Without those, <Term id="imitation-learning">imitation learning</Term> is the practical first use of demonstrations. In simulation, RL can stand in for scarce demonstrations: SimpleVLA-RL lifted OpenVLA-OFT trained on one demonstration per task from 48.9% to 96.9% average LIBERO success <Cite id="simplevla-rl-2025" />.

edits.before:
For a first serious project, spend the opening phase on replayable data and a deterministic evaluation harness. Build behavior cloning next. Add action chunks or a multimodal head only when the baseline exposes the need. Add a VLA when semantic transfer is part of the task. Add RL only when the reward, coverage and reset loop are real.

The sequence is conservative because robot experiments are expensive and confounded. Its benefit is speed: every stage produces an artifact you keep, and every added method answers a failure you can already name.
edits.after: Build replayable data and a deterministic evaluation harness, then behavior cloning; add chunks when the baseline needs them, a VLA for semantic transfer, and RL once reward, coverage and resets are real. The tutorial provides ready-to-use LeRobot examples <Cite id="robot-learning-tutorial-2025" />.

edits.before:
A <Term id="vision-language-action-model">vision-language-action (VLA)</Term> model is a robot policy built by adapting a vision-language model to output robot actions. The modules so far covered policies trained from scratch on robot data alone: [behavior cloning](/manipulation/bc-foundations), [ACT](/manipulation/action-chunking), and [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy). The VLA line changes the starting point. Instead of training a policy from nothing, take a model that already understands images and language from web-scale pretraining, and teach it to emit robot actions. The design question that defines this lineage is how to get actions out of a model whose output space is text.

The interactive below is an illustrative seven-coordinate action sequence; it is neither a recorded rollout nor a literal tokenizer vocabulary. It places values in 256 uniform bins on a fixed normalized interval and uses synthetic token labels. Drag “Moment in the movement” to see each motion’s nudge land in one of the 256 slots and become a word; the motion buttons and the full 256-slot strip are under “Adjust more”, and the reconstruction error is under “How this was made”. Quantization discards within-bin detail, but error can be zero when a value equals its reconstructed bin center. OpenVLA’s actual bin bounds use training-data quantiles; the toy does not estimate those statistics. <Cite id="openvla-2024" /> Move to another moment and the assigned slot and reconstruction error both track it.
edits.after: A <Term id="vision-language-action-model">vision-language-action (VLA)</Term> model is a robot policy built by adapting a vision-language model to output robot actions. Earlier [behavior cloning](/manipulation/bc-foundations/) and [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy/) learned from robot data alone. It starts from a model pretrained on web-scale images and text, and the design question is how to get actions out of a model that outputs text <Cite id="rt2-2023" />.

edits.before: RT-1 (2022) combines an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet with a pretrained instruction embedding and FiLM language conditioning. It tokenizes six images: TokenLearner reduces 81 visual tokens per image to eight, yielding 48 tokens for an eight-layer decoder-only transformer with 19M parameters. The paper reports 35M parameters for the full system. <Cite id="rt1-2022" />
edits.after: RT-1 (2022) combines an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet <Cite id="efficientnet-2019" />, a pretrained instruction embedding and FiLM language conditioning <Cite id="film-2018" />. TokenLearner <Cite id="tokenlearner-2021" /> cuts each of six images from 81 visual tokens to eight, giving 48 tokens for an eight-layer, 19M-parameter decoder-only transformer; the full system has 35M parameters <Cite id="rt1-2022" />.

edits.before: Its 11 action coordinates comprise seven arm variables (translation, rotation and gripper opening), three base variables (x, y and yaw), and a switch between arm control, base control and episode termination. Each variable is discretized into 256 bins uniformly spaced within its bounds; training uses categorical cross-entropy over action tokens. <Cite id="rt1-2022" />
edits.after: Its 11 action coordinates are seven arm variables (translation, rotation and gripper opening), three base variables (x, y and yaw) and a switch between arm control, base control and episode termination. Each is discretized into 256 bins spaced uniformly within its bounds and trained with categorical cross-entropy <Cite id="rt1-2022" />. Drag “Moment in the movement” to watch each motion's value land in one of 256 bins.

edits.before: The paper reports roughly 130k training episodes covering more than 700 tasks, collected over 17 months with 13 robots, and 3,000 real-world evaluation trials. Its authors argue that generalization requires both scale and breadth, with sufficiently connected tasks to learn reusable patterns. That is their dataset argument; pooling arbitrary demonstrations carries no guarantee of improving every task. <Cite id="rt1-2022" />
edits.after: RT-1 reports about 130k episodes over more than 700 tasks, collected over 17 months with 13 robots, and 3,000 real-world evaluation trials. The authors argue that generalization needs both scale and breadth, with sufficiently connected tasks <Cite id="rt1-2022" />.

edits.before: RT-1 reports a 3 Hz robot-control rate and predicts the next action instead of an action chunk. Its implementation uses a fixed wait after capturing the state to keep action timing consistent; the paper's implementation details give 280 ms as the maximum observed latency of all components. These are settings of the reported system and set no universal limit on tokenized policies. Its visual and language encoders are pretrained, so describing the whole system as trained on robot data alone would also be misleading. <Cite id="rt1-2022" />
edits.after: RT-1 commands actions at 3 Hz and predicts the next action, with no chunk. A fixed wait of 280 ms, the maximum observed latency of all components, keeps action timing consistent <Cite id="rt1-2022" />.

edits.before: RT-2 (2023) attacked the knowledge problem directly <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. It skips bolting a robot head onto a <Term id="vision-language-model">vision-language model</Term>: each action dimension is discretized into 256 bins, and the bin indices are serialized into the VLM's existing token stream as strings. The two backbones handle the vocabulary differently, which is a detail worth keeping: PaLI-X already has a token for every integer up to 1000, so bins map onto existing number tokens, while PaLM-E overwrites the 256 least frequently used tokens with the action vocabulary. The backbone (PaLI-X or PaLM-E, up to 55B parameters) is then co-fine-tuned on a mixture of robot trajectories and the original web vision-language data. The authors report that mixing the original web data with robot data during co-fine-tuning produces more generalizable policies than fine-tuning on robot data alone <Cite id="rt2-2023" />.
edits.after: RT-2 (2023) brings web knowledge into control <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. Each action dimension is discretized into 256 bins, and the bin indices are serialized as strings into a <Term id="vision-language-model">vision-language model</Term>'s token stream. PaLI-X already has a token for every integer up to 1000, so bins map onto number tokens, while PaLM-E overwrites its 256 least frequently used tokens. The backbone, up to 55B parameters, is co-fine-tuned on robot trajectories and the original web vision-language data, which the authors report generalizes better than robot data alone <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. PaLM-E had already shown positive transfer from joint web-scale language, vision and visual-language training <Cite id="palm-e-2023" />.

edits.before: RT-2 separates emergent object-choice behavior, such as selecting the smallest object or the one closest to another, from its additional chain-of-thought experiment. For the latter, the authors fine-tune a variant with an intermediate natural-language plan before the action tokens; their concrete example is “Instruction: I’m hungry. Plan: pick rxbar chocolate.” The abstract also gives choosing a rock as an improvised hammer as a multi-stage semantic-reasoning example. This is more specific than claiming that ordinary action decoding automatically supplies a reasoning trace. <Cite id="rt2-2023" />
edits.after: RT-2 also shows emergent object choice, such as picking the smallest object or the one closest to another, and multi-stage semantic reasoning, such as using a rock as an improvised hammer. A separate variant writes a natural-language plan before the action tokens: "Instruction: I’m hungry. Plan: pick rxbar chocolate." <Cite id="rt2-2023" /> Gemini Robotics 1.5 interleaves actions with natural-language reasoning <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />.

edits.before: In their May 2025 research note, Danny Driess and colleagues at Physical Intelligence argue that this tokenized representation “is not suitable for high-frequency, precise, or fluent motions,” citing their π0 and π0-FAST experiments. Their analogy is “controlling your arm by verbally saying which muscles should contract.” This is the authors’ stated assessment of the representation; no independently established impossibility result stands behind it. <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />
edits.after: In a May 2025 research note, Danny Driess and colleagues at Physical Intelligence call this tokenization "not suitable for high-frequency, precise, or fluent motions," citing their π0 and π0-FAST experiments. They liken it to "controlling your arm by verbally saying which muscles should contract" <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />. The same lab's FAST paper locates the failure in simple per-dimension, per-timestep binning; its compressed tokens match diffusion VLAs on 10k hours of robot data while training up to 5 times faster <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />. VLA-0 writes actions as plain text and, on LIBERO, outperforms π0.5-KI, OpenVLA-OFT and SmolVLA trained on the same robot data <Cite id="vla-0-2025" />.

## Where this leaves the field

These studies demonstrate particular transfers from web pretraining and pooled robot data; universal improvement from scale alone is a stronger claim than they support. Their action interfaces, data mixtures, input modalities and execution protocols differ. Read the reported token-generation rates and robot-control rates separately, and compare results only with their task and evaluation settings attached. <Cite id="rt2-2023" /> <Cite id="openvla-2024" />
edits.after: Action interfaces, data mixtures, inputs and execution protocols differ across these studies, so read token-generation and robot-control rates separately <Cite id="rt2-2023" /> <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. With LIBERO near its ceiling, ranking needs harder tests ([evaluation crisis](/data-hardware/evaluation-crisis/)): RoboArena compares generalist policies in double-blind pairs on DROID robots at seven institutions <Cite id="roboarena-2025" />, and SIMPLER's simulated scores correlate with real performance <Cite id="simpler-2024" />.

edits.before: Treat “VLA” as two decisions behind one label. The first is the prior: which visual, language and robot experience the backbone brings to the task. The second is the control interface: what action the model emits, over what horizon, in which frame and at what measured rate. A large semantic prior can improve instruction following while a poor action interface still makes the system unusable at contact. OpenVLA-OFT is the clean example because changing the decoding and action head materially changed both throughput and success without replacing the underlying VLA <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />.
edits.after: A VLA is two decisions. The prior is the visual, language and robot experience in the backbone; the control interface is the action, horizon, frame and measured rate. A large prior can improve instruction following while a poor interface fails at contact: OFT changed both throughput and success without replacing OpenVLA <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />. Before choosing a checkpoint, write down the required semantic novelty, available embodiment data, action contract and latency budget. Pick the prior with the [foundation-model guide](/manipulation/foundation-models/) and the output with the [action-space guide](/manipulation/action-spaces/), then compare only models whose contracts match; [generalist policies](/manipulation/generalist-policies/) and [RL fine-tuning](/manipulation/rl-finetuning/) cover the rest.
